speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPORT ON ORGANIZATION OF COMMITTEE ON EUROPEAN RELIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it might be of interest to hon. members of the house to inform them-they have no doubt learned of it through the newspapers-that the organization meeting of the Canadian national European flood relief committee was held at Government House on Friday afternoon under the chairmanship of His Excellency the Governor General. As hon. members know, that committee comprises the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, four other members of this house and the two lady members of the other house of parliament. Every one of the ten provincial premiers has welcomed the opportunity of serving on the committee, and the campaign has their warm support. It is being started today in all ten Canadian provinces but the national committee does not intend to organize the campaigns locally. It is counting upon the
welfare or service cluns in the various localities to set up their local organizations. But in handling a matter of that character, it is very important that there be co-ordination and that only the supplies that are really needed are sent forward and that they are sent to the places where they are most urgently needed. The Red Cross has its officials in Europe now, and the offices of the high commissioner in London and the embassies at The Hague and at Brussels are in close touch with the government relief agencies of these three countries, as well as in close touch with the officials of the Canadian Red Cross. Miss Margaret Wilson, executive secretary, is at present in London and Colonel Walter Reynolds, national director of disaster services, is still at The Hague. These officials are keeping in very close touch with what the local relief organizations are doing.
The high commissioner's office and the two embassies are making cable facilities available to these representatives of the Red Cross so that they can make daily reports to the central organization here in Canada to be sure that the right kind of supplies will be provided, to the extent to which that can be done from Canada, and that they will be provided in the places where they are most urgently required. It would seem that the immediate urgent requirements for food or medical supplies or even for large amounts of clothing have been met, and that the big problem will be the permanent or semipermanent rehabilitation of the very large numbers who have suffered so severely from this flood disaster.
I think that through the activities of the Red Cross, and the assistance they are thus getting overseas, we will be kept well informed as to what will comply with that resolution adopted unanimously by the House of Commons the other day to give concrete examples of our sympathy in the most helpful way possible.

Perhaps this would be the appropriate place in the proceedings to raise a matter that came to my attention through a
1950	HOUSE OF
University Scholarships report in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, February 14. In that issue of the Citizen there is a report of a visit the previous day by representatives of the national executive of the National Federation of University Students. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is reported as informing them, and I quote:
The Prime Minister said he had been attempting since last fall to set up a Canadian committee to administer such scholarships, but had failed in the attempt.
The reference is to a request that was made that the government implement certain recommendations of the Massey report in regard to scholarships. The reply given to the student representatives indicates that the government has reached some decision. Since this is a subject in regard to which hon. members in every part of the house are interested and upon which they have been receiving representations, I would ask the Prime Minister whether he could tell the house what the decision is that the government has reached, and also indicate the nature of the difficulties to which he has referred.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid that that report in the Citizen is rather more than second hand; it must be third or fourth hand, because it is not an accurate report of what transpired. I assured these young people that I had always had a great interest in university work, and that though for something over eleven years now my active connection with universities had not been as intimate as it was before, I was still very much interested. I said that personally I felt we had had an illustration, in the success of the veterans who got university training after the last war, that anything that was expended in that way was a national investment and brought returns even to the Canadian treasury.
I informed them that I had been concerned about this part of the Massey report, and I have been endeavouring to make such inquiries as would have enabled me to make a recommendation to my colleagues about the set-up of a Canadian council. Unfortunately, those I had approached for that purpose had found that they could not at the present time fall in with our plans, and I have not yet been able to co-ordinate in my own mind the kind of thing I could recommend to my colleagues. I felt that that was something that would necessarily have to precede the establishment of a system of scholarships, because I thought a system of scholarships would have to be administered by the kind of organization that would be quite divorced from any suggestion of political patronage.
TMr. Drew.]

I told them that I realized that their generation of students was advancing, and that they were very anxious to have it done at the earliest possible moment. I had found, however, it had not been possible for me to co-ordinate anything that I could put before my colleagues for implementation during this session of parliament.

In view of the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has made, might I suggest that there are meetings of representatives of the universities before which a suggestion of this kind could be placed and doubtless recommendations made that would be acceptable to those universities, without any of the difficulties to which the Prime Minister has referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had some experience
last year, Mr. Speaker, with the recommendations made by the university council about the grants to universities. A solution was found for last year, but we were informed that it was only for one year that that solution was being accepted. It has not been possible as yet to find a solution acceptable for this year. These are matters in which the hon. gentleman and I, and every other hon. member in the house, are deeply concerned. But we are also deeply concerned with avoiding the doing of anything to countenance this suggestion that we are trying to inject ourselves into the domain of education. No one wants to do that. Everyone wants to leave that responsibility of the provincial administration as the fathers of confederation intended it should be.
It is not easy to do anything at all that does have a bearing upon the educational problem without there being misgivings in many quarters. I hope that will not always be so, and I hope that as it was possible to find a solution last year it will be possible to find a solution this year and that those solutions, one after the other, may establish a precedent that will allow these desirable things to be done without there being additional misgivings about interference by the central government with matters of provincial jurisdiction and responsibility.

I do not wish to extend this matter beyond this point, but I want to make the observation that the granting of scholarships is, of course, different from the granting of financial assistance direct to the universities. There are scholarships now being awarded in certain connections by agencies of the dominion government. I understood the recommendation was that these should be extended, and that does not bring the government in direct contact with the administration of any university.
Might 1 ask a supplementary question?
Order, order.

I too have my rights in asking questions. In view of the question asked by myself as reported at page 1729 of Hansard and the answer given at that time by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), that the government is continuing to study the recommendation on scholarships, I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) whether consideration has been given by the government to this matter as a whole as well as the consideration which he himself says he has given to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has on the order paper four questions which actually consist of 22 separate queries and which refer to the A.V. Roe program. This program has also been recently referred to in the house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I believe that I can make one statement which will answer these and any similar questions, and at the same time clarify the situation which exists at A.V. Roe.
After A.V. Roe established in Canada on December 1, 1945, the company was given the primary task of developing a long-range, all-weather interceptor and turbo-jet engine for the R.C.A.F. They were also asked to develop a jet transport plane, overhaul and modify world war II Lancasters, and in addition were given a number of lesser projects.
Gas Turbine Development
In November, 1945, Turbo Research Limited, a crown company, was authorized to proceed with the design and construction of the TR-3 Chinook. Detail design of this power plant was under way when the assets of Turbo Research Limited were transferred to A.V. Roe Canada Limited in 1946. The Chinook was originally intended as the power plant for a R.C.A.F. fighter. Changed requirements produced the specification for the Orenda.

The Chinook, a 2,900 pound thrust machine, was completed to provide experience in design, development and manufacturing problems. The Orenda specification called for an engine of 6,500 pound thrust, equal to that of the largest engines then in design in the United States and the United Kingdom.
The Orenda first ran in February, 1949, thirty months from commencement of design. The gas turbine staff was then about 800, and expenditures on the Orenda project to the end of March, 1949, amounted to $3,917,900. With the running of the first engine, the development phase commenced. This has extended over four years, and five distinguishable versions of the engine have now passed the development phase. These are:
Series 1-Original design.
Series 2-Modification to permit three point suspension system, to increase strength, reduce weight, and make fuselage installations easier.
Series 8-Modified compressor to improve acceleration characteristics.
Series 9-Version for CF-100 Mark 4.
Series 10-Version for F-86.
All of these engines are in the 6,0006,500 pound thrust category. In addition, the series 11 engine (7,500 pound thrust) has run in lash-up form, and the basic scheming on the series 12 engine, with a further increase in thrust is complete.
The $30,274,199 spent on the Orenda over the last four years is described as a development expense. In fact, however, all engineering expenses, some of which would have been charged to production, have been carried on this contract. The expenditures have supported an engineering department large enough to carry out the production activities, produce the variants of the basic engine described above, and work on certain more advanced developments. Finally, engineering expenses include the operation of the experimental or model shop, and also the Nobel facility, a laboratory which carries out research and development of turbines, compressors, and combustion systems.
The Orenda engine series 11 will be superior to the present production versions of engines designed for similar purposes in other countries. We are satisfied that the Orenda series 12 engine will meet our requirements for some years, and be competitive with foreign engines.
Gas Turbine Production
The prototype Orenda first ran in February, 1949. At December 31, 1952, expenditures on tooling were $15,029,350. This figure covers preproduction and production tooling for all series of the engine.

Total expenditures on production have now reached $38,785,500, with $17,839,300 representing the value of engines delivered, $20,946,300 the value of engines in final assembly, parts completed and in process, progress payments to suppliers, materials inventory and mill supplies. For this expenditure, 96 engines were delivered at December 31, 1952.
The first twelve Orendas were produced in the development shop, on limited tooling, to supply urgently needed engines for early aircraft. In addition, the two changes of engine production location, first from the experimental shop to the pilot line in the aircraft plant and then to the new engine plant, have had an adverse effect on costs.
The construction of the engine plant was authorized in October, 1950. An eight-month delay in completion of the plant proper resulted from the shortage of steel at that time. In March, 1952, only 10 per cent of the machine tools were installed. The plant can scarcely be considered to have begun operations before June, 1952, when 60 per cent of the machine tools were installed, while the assembly shops were not moved until July, 1952, and heat treating facilities until November of last year. Under these circumstances, and considering the problems of setting up subcontractors' facilities, the performance has been good.
The Orenda series 2 was the first production engine. This passed its type test in February, 1952, and is now out of production. The series 8 and series 10 passed their type tests in January of this year and these are the engines presently in production. The series 9 is to be introduced during the summer of 1953.
Airframe Development
In October, 1946, a contract was executed with A. V. Roe for the design and construction of two prototypes of the CF-100, plus one static test airframe. In January, 1950, the first prototype flew. This was a Mark 1 aeroplane, fitted with Rolls-Royce Avons. Cumulative expenditures to March 31, 1950, were $5,131,754.68.
To the present, cumulative expenditures on development of the airframe have amounted to $11,784,400, an increase of $6,652,646 since March, 1950. Variants of the aeroplane obtained for this expenditure are:
(1)	CF-100 Mark 2-powered by Orenda series 1; no armament.
(2)	CF-100 Mark 3-powered by the Orenda series 2 and series 8, and armed with eight 50 calibre machine guns and APG 33 radar.
Questions
(3)	CF-100 Mark 4-powered by the Orenda series 9 and armed with 50 calibre machine guns, air to air rockets, and APG 40 radar.
The development of the Mark 4 control system for firing the armament is not yet completed.
I have already mentioned two of the differences between these four marks of the CF-100. One is the different series of engines and the other is the different weapon systems. Externally, all Marks are similar. The structure has undergone considerable development, beginning with the first static test in March, 1950. It is expected that the final proving of the structure to Mark 4 loads will be complete in March, 1953. This long time results from the growth of all-up weight (about 50 per cent), as well as from deficiencies in the original design. In addition, systems have been altered: for example, the control system has been changed to obtain improved flying qualities; hydraulic and electrical systems were altered as a result of increased demands and a desire to clean up the original design.
I have mentioned the deficiency in the original design, a subject that has been given a great deal of publicity. The facts were that in November, 1951, during R.C.A.F. proving flights, a failure developed in the ring connecting the fuselage to the front spar. This necessitated a redesign of this structure which has now been successfully accomplished. Vigorous rectification commenced with the reorganization of the engineering department, and progress since then has been good. No time has been lost on the delivery schedule of the Mark 4 (rocket firing) aircraft, as the delivery date of this aircraft is determined by the weapons system, which is being produced in the United States. The delay in the Mark 3 program amounted to 4 - 6 months. It is not possible to separate out the costs of this element of the CF-100 development program. The only other two seat fighters in the same class as the CF-100 have also suffered structural deficiencies which have caused serious delays.
Summarizing the CF-100 development, this aircraft appears to be superior to its only immediate competitor, although it is inevitable that in time it will be made obsolete by the introduction of improved jet bombers.
Airframe Production
In May, 1949, seven months before the flight of the first development prototype, a contract was issued for ten preproduction fighter aircraft. In June, 1951, the first of these aircraft flew, the last in October, 1952.

Questions
The first five of the aircraft were Mark 2, the next four were Mark 3, and the tenth was the Mark 4 weapons system prototype.
The first production order for the CF-100 was given in October, 1950. The first production aeroplane was delivered in November, 1952, 25 months from the placing of the contract. This length of time resulted primarily from the difficulties encountered with the structure of the aeroplane, to which I have already made reference. The Mark 3 aeroplane is now in production and 70 fighters of this mark, fitted with 50 calibre guns, will be produced. Volume production of the CF-100 Mark 4 will begin late this summer.
Tooling expenditures to the present have amounted to $15,882,450. Total production cost of the 16 aircraft delivered up to December 31, 1952, against the preproduction and production program, is divided as follows:
(1)	Aircraft manufactured, $27,248,300.
(2)	Mill supply inventory, raw material inventory, work in process, $25,788,800.
(3)	Payments to subcontractors and supplies, $4,183,500.
(4)	Ground handling equipment, maintenance tools, publications, etc., $2,582,400.
At the present time, there are approximately 14,000 persons employed at A.V. Roe, and it is not expected that this number will increase significantly during the course of the present program. Last summer there was some concern that there were more people on the A.V. Roe payroll than production warranted. I think probably that, to some extent, this was true. I am satisfied that this condition no longer exists. The under-utilization of the Avro labour force was the result of a number of factors:
(a)	Hiring was done in advance of the work to be performed because many of the new employees required training on the job to fit them for full production work. At the same time, production in some cases did not get underway according to schedule, and, correctly anticipating a tight labour market, Avro was hesitant about letting these workers go.
(b)	The very magnitude of the build-up in employment, required to meet production schedules, made it almost inevitable that some labour inefficiency would result. In 1952, for example, Avro hired some 9,000 new employees during a period when total employment showed a net increase of just over 6,000 workers. Now that intake can be slowed down substantially, greater emphasis can be placed on improved selection of workers, with a resulting increase in labour efficiency.

(c)	The physical problem involved in bringing a large amount of new plant into operation, and in transferring and rearranging machines and workers, caused some reduction in the efficiency of the labour force.
(d)	The difficulties encountered in getting the CF-100 centre section redesigned and cleared for production resulted in less than optimum utilization of the labour force. This is no longer a problem.
In considering the A. V. Roe program, comparisons are often made with the F-86 program at Canadair. In making such comparisons, however, there are several factors that must be kept in mind.
1.	The CF-100 is one of the biggest and heaviest fighter aircraft being produced today. It weighs approximately 17 tons. That is heavier than the 21 passenger DC-3 transport, and about two and a half times as heavy as a standard fighter such as the Sabre. If comparisons are to be made, this additional weight and the increased complexity must be kept in mind.
2.	A. V. Roe has designed, developed, and is now producing both the airframe and engine. It is true that development costs have been heavy, but it must be remembered that in manufacturing a plane developed in another country, as we are doing at Canadair, we are faced with heavy licence fees that are in reality a payment which we are making to support the development staff of an aircraft company in another country.
3.	We were able to give Canadair a sufficiently large order to permit them to set up an economic production line, which they have done with great efficiency and which will enable Canada to fill its NATO commitments in the time allotted. On the other hand, the CF-100 will be the basis of our home defence and we are most concerned that it does not become obsolescent too rapidly. Consequently, it has been our policy not to load the air force with the earlier marks of the CF-100, and to place a minimum order for the Mark 3 in order to await the Mark 4. We will place a heavier order for this aeroplane, thus permitting more efficient production at A. V. Roe.
There has been some recent speculation concerning fighters of advanced designs. This is a subject on which I can say very little without compromising military security. I can assure hon. members, however, that we are constantly studying new concepts and new designs. In doing so, we are anxious to examine designs which are available to us from other countries. However, we have what I consider a good design and development organization at A. V. Roe and, naturally, we will not overlook their talents.

During the period of "cold war" such as we are experiencing at the present time, it is a matter of serious concern to the R.C.A.F. to keep its equipment modern without retiring serviceable but obsolete aircraft. In war, this problem does not generally exist as the aircraft are consumed in service before they become obsolete. In peacetime, however, it is very difficult to keep the force modern without making frequent changes in the production line and producing relatively small numbers of different marks of aircraft. When the R.C.A.F. is up to strength in aircraft, it is our intention to then provide new aircraft at the attrition rate of those that are in the service. This will mean a small yearly volume of production, but obviously they must be of the latest possible types.
In conclusion, I am satisfied that our program at A. V. Roe is now in good shape. As a country inexperienced in aircraft design and development, it was natural that we should experience difficulties and delays which are, in fact, characteristic of the aeroplane business. It might have been expected that, in our case, delays would have been more protracted than those experienced in countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States, where they have not only a well established aircraft industry, but also the supporting industry which is so essential. Considering the Orenda program, A. V. Roe's record in getting into production compares well with that of other companies. This is a particularly outstanding achievement when one considers that, not only did we have to build the new plant at A. V. Roe, but also had to bring into being more than a dozen new industries that are producing in Canada, for the first time, technical components which will not only serve our aircraft industry but also our general economy. A. V. Roe's record on the CF-100, which is our first all-Canadian fighter, has been a credit to the company.

Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the next order of business, in view of the number of questions that have been asked on the matter previously I should like to read to the house a statement I intend to give to the press with regard to butter. It is as follows:
Commenting on the butter situation the Minister of Agriculture stated today that the government still owned more than 29,000,000 pounds of butter and that this supply was regarded as being sufficient to meet all needs until the new production season opens up. He also stated that the government butter would be sold at a basic price of 62 cents per pound for solids in Quebec and Ontario.
And at comparable prices elsewhere.
The only condition attached to sales would be that the buyer would make immediate delivery to retailers and that the mark-up for cutting, wrapping and distributing would be fair and reasonable. The minister pointed out that due to the wide variety of conditions governing retail trade it was very difficult to name a mark-up that would govern all situations. He did say that in many of the larger centres a price of 62 cents for solids in the past had enabled a large section of the retail trade to sell at retail prices of 65 cents and 66 cents, but he recognized that these prices could not be made to govern cases where special services were required. Nevertheless it is expected that there will be full co-operation from the trade and that fair prices will prevail.
The minister also observed that butter production at the present time is somewhat higher than it was last year at the same date. In addition, the point of low production for the year has already been passed and fresh supplies will increase from week to week. For this reason and because of the availability of government stocks of stored butter consumers can be assured of ample supplies at 62 cents wholesale for solids for the remainder of this year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before I adjourned the debate

on Friday evening I was drawing to the attention of the house the desirability of unanimity in the face of a common enemy so far as Canadian foreign affairs are concerned. I pointed out that because of statements, however veiled, that had been made in the house by the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) and statements that had been made throughout the country by another member of that party, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), this no longer is a fact. It may be a fact in the house, yet it is unfair to the Canadian people that they be given the impression that the House of Commons is not in any way divided on the question of participation in the United Nations and in world affairs.
I drew the attention of the house to a statement by the member for Peace River (Mr. Low), in which he said, and I quote from page 1881 of Hansard for February 12, 1953:
But, Mr. Speaker, when the full history of these times is written, when all of the facts have been brought to light, there will be many people who will say that the past two presidents of the United States have been the great betrayers of humanity.
At that time I was asked by the hon. member to read on. I did, Mr. Speaker, and to my great astonishment I found the following on the same page of Hansard:
To be charitable, as I ought to be, I will say that some of those decisions made at Yalta and Potsdam, some of the secret understandings and agreements that were had with Stalin, may have been made in good faith.
I may say that at both of these conferences the Right Hon. Winston Churchill was present, and in addition at the Potsdam conference there were well known figures in the political life of Britain and the United States. At the Potsdam conference the following were present: Harry S. Truman, J. Stalin, Winston Churchill and the secretaries of the three governments, Mr. James Byrnes, Mr. Molotov and Mr. Anthony Eden. Are these the gentlemen who we are to believe have been treacherous in their decisions? When the history is written, Mr. Speaker, regardless of whether it is written by fascist sympathizers or true historians, as one Canadian citizen I shall refuse to believe that there was any treachery by western representatives during the time these agreements were made. Mistakes may have been made, but to say that they were treacherous mistakes is certainly not a becoming statement.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr Jutras) read into the record an article which the hon. member for Macleod agreed that he had written. In this article, which is supposed

to be an honest appraisal of the United Nations, the hon. member said:
-truth is still our weapon, but let us have the whole truth. The fact of the matter is that this United Nations is largely a socialist-communist organization.
The hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Beyer-stein), a member of the Social Credit party, was a parliamentary observer at the United Nations, and it would be interesting to hear from him whether, during his visit there, he found that he was associating largely with communist-socialists. I believe that quite the contrary was true. We have a continuous opposition from the Soviet bloc which represents five votes. If that bloc were given the same rights in privileges as the United States, with the large number of states compared with the socialist states, I am sure it would have only one vote and that would leave the communist world with but one vote in the United Nations.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that because of the rules of the house it is impossible for me to move that this house register in the affirmative its decision to carry on its allegiance to the United Nations as a world organization. I believe that in the interest of the Canadian public generally that should be done before this session is prorogued.
On Friday I mentioned that there was one particular matter coming before the United Nations which I believed is of great importance. It was referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in his address which opened this debate. I believe we all appreciate the fact that the minister, now that he is president of the general assembly, cannot speak out in the same terms and with the same force as he did on earlier occasions. However, during his address he stated, and I quote from page 1849 of Hansard for February 11, 1953:
It is probable, however, that there will be further far-reaching discussions at later sessions of the general assembly on the reconciliation of domestic jurisdiction as laid down in the charter with the claim that the United Nations is competent to consider and to intervene in any question which anyone may wish to put on the agenda. There is probably no more important long-range problem facing the United Nations general assembly than this.
In his address during this debate the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) suggested that a committee should be set up to discuss the charter of the United Nations and to make recommendations. Should such a committee be set up, I feel that this is one very important question with which it should deal. The committee which will discuss chese estimates should also consider this
External Affairs
very important question. Reference is made to this matter in article 1, subsection 7, of the charter, and I quote:
Nothing contained in the present charter shall authorize the United Nations to intervene in matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state or shall require the members to submit such matters to settlement under the present charter; but this principle shall not prejudice the application of enforcement measures under chapter VII.
In an earlier address 'the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) criticized the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) for the position the Canadian delegation took on the question of apartheid in South Africa. I believe that this question is perhaps a basic one with respect to United Nations authority. We should consider the United Nations as united nations rather than a united states. If we are to deal with minority groups in any and every state, then the United Nations would be almost ineffective in that it would be cluttered up with every conceivable jurisdictional question, questions of domestic jurisdiction, which many nations themselves cannot solve. If these questions were brought before the world forum, it would simply confuse the issues instead of settling them. However abhorrent the South African government's decision is to us as individuals, there is perhaps much to be said and much consideration should be given to the various problems of that country.
It may be noted that the Russian delegation were all in favour of this type of intervention. But as to a nation which is reported to have 20 million political prisoners within its boundaries, what can be said of its right to vote condemning a smaller country for its particular political problems respecting minorities?

Since the motion was to refer the estimates to the standing committee on external affairs,
1 had expected that a pronouncement by each of the leaders might have been sufficient so that the estimates could have gone to the committee and the minister could have been free to go to the United Nations as I understand he desires to do at the earliest possible moment.
At the outset of my speech, however, I wish to say that I too have visited the United Nations-as have many others in this parliament. It was my privilege to go with the delegation, as one of the parliamentary advisers, last year when we met in Paris, France. I must say that I enjoyed my work greatly. I did not have a great deal to say, but as a result of my observations, I would say I was pleased with the way the Canadian delegation took up their task and worked. I was particularly impressed by and pleased with the staff of brilliant young men the minister had at Paris at the time. I have no criticism whatsoever to make of the staff in the Department of External Affairs. I believe they are doing an excellent job in attempting to achieve the policy which is laid down by the government itself. I would say the same thing for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). While at times we may rise and exercise our democratic right of criticism, we want the minister to know that, as far as we are concerned, and as far as our relationship with him goes, we are behind him in his desire to accomplish that which he set out to do. We do not always agree with government policy in respect of foreign affairs.
I might also say this, if it is not premature to do so. Should the minister reach higher levels of responsibility in the United Nations, we want him to know that this group will be behind him in the exercise of those responsibilities. Whether or not he will eventually be in a position of determining policy, I do not know; but as to any responsibility that might come to him in giving guidance to

such a vast organization, we want him to know that we will stand with him in his work. We are not opposed to the United Nations as an instrument for the furtherance of international cooperation. We do feel, however, that there is definite evidence of intrigue in high places which is undermining the sovereignty of the freedom loving nations of the world, and which will ultimately enslave the people through world government over which they will have no control.

He did not quote that part of my article.
Then, I should like to deal with what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). When I listened to him on Friday evening, when he commenced the speech he finished today, I must say that he sounded more like a kindergarten boy attempting to instruct his teacher, when he proceeded to level his criticism against my leader. I will read the entire quotation as it appears in the speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) as reported at page 1881 of Hansard:
Consequently, in so far as Mr. Truman did meet international challenges during the years he occupied the presidential office, I join with the minister in paying tribute. But, Mr. Speaker, when the full history of these times is written, when all of the facts have been brought to light, there will be many people who will say that the past two presidents of the United States have been the great betrayers of humanity. To be charitable, as I ought to be, I will say that some of those decisions made at Yalta and Potsdam, some of the secret understandings and agreements that were had with Stalin, may have been made in good faith; but the very best anyone can say is that they indicated a most serious lack of foresight and judgment on the part of those two presidents. It may have been that they listened too much to unsound advice from men like Alger Hiss, but they will not on that account be able to escape the judgment of history.
I should like to make it clear that in using those words the other day in the house the hon. member for Peace River did not, himself, condemn President Truman and President Roosevelt. He said distinctly that when the full history is written many people will say that the past two presidents have been the great betrayers of humanity. My leader does not make statements that he cannot prove.
I wonder now if I may quote what was said by Congressman B. Carroll Reese of Tennessee when speaking in the House of

Representatives on March 19,	1951, as
recorded at pages A-1564 to A-1568 of the Congressional Record. He said:
We could have easily gotten to Berlin first. But our troops were first halted at the Elbe. They were then withdrawn from that river in a wide circle- far enough westward to make Stalin a present of the great Zeiss optical and precision instrument works at Jena, the most important VI and V2 rocket laboratory and production plant in Nord-hausen, and the vital underground jet plant in Kahla. Everywhere we surrendered to the soviets intact, thousands of German planes, including great masses of jet fighters ready for assembly, as well as research centres, rocket developments, scientific personnel, and other military treasures.
When it was all over, a large part of the formidable Russian militarism of today was clearly marked "made in America" or "donated by America from Germany". But where Roosevelt left off, President Truman resumed.
At Potsdam, Truman, maintaining intact Roosevelt's iron curtain of secret diplomacy, played fast and loose with American honour and security. He agreed to an enlargement of the boundaries of a Poland already delivered by Roosevelt and Churchill to Russian control through addition of areas that had, for centuries, been occupied by Germans or people of German origin. Some 14 million persons were brutally expelled from their homes with the confiscation of virtually all their property. Only 10 million finally reached the American, French and British zones of Germany. Four million mysteriously disappeared, though the finger points toward Russian atrocities. Thus Truman approved one of the great mass deportations in history, which for sheer cruelty is a dark page in the annals of history.
At Potsdam, Truman also sanctioned Russian acquisition of Eastern Germany, the food-bin of that nation before the war. It then became impossible for the remaining German economy in British, French, and American hands to feed its people. Germany, like Japan, also went on our bounty rolls.
Like Roosevelt, Truman did not neglect to build up Russian military strength when his opportunity came at Potsdam. He provided her with more factories, machines and military equipment, though at the time he attended Potsdam, Truman knew that through lend-lease we had already dangerously expanded Russia's military might and that, in addition, we had given the soviets some 15,000 planes-many of them of our latest type-and 7,000 tanks.
That is from a speech by Representative B. Carroll Reese.

What he said was like a mild and perfumed lovetap in comparison with what millions of betrayed people are thinking and saying. What is more, during the election campaign in the United States, hundreds of speakers over the air and on the hustings said things that make my leader's words look weak, pale and anaemic. Let me read from the platform of the Republican party concerning these agreements. That is what it said:
The government of the United States, under Republican leadership, will repudiate all commitments contained in secret understandings such as those at Yalta which aid communist enslavement. It will make clear, on the highest authority of the President and the Congress, that United States policy, as one of its peaceful purposes, looks happily forward to the genuine independence of those captive peoples.
The hon. member for Kootenay East tried to bolster up his case by pointing out that Churchill was at Yalta and Potsdam. I suppose he wanted to convey that if anyone was condemning Presidents Roosevelt and Truman he would also have to condemn Churchill. I should like to point out that Mr. Churchill was very alarmed at President Roosevelt's silly infatuation for Stalin and his reckless serving of the interests of world communism. On October 21,	1942, Mr. Churchill wrote to the British foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, as follows:
It would be a measureless disaster if Russian barbarism overlaid the culture and independence of the ancient states of Europe.
From all one can gather from the bits and pieces that have dropped from the lips and pen of Churchill, that gentleman did what he could to oppose Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Truman in their recklessness. I would point out also to hon. members that Churchill felt that an invasion of the Balkans was to be preferred to head-on attempting to invade Germany by way of the northern counties of France. Roosevelt opposed this request, it appears, for no other reason than to please

External Affairs
Stalin. In fact, Churchill evidently put up with a great deal of indignity and had to agree to many strategically unsound policies to prevent the clique of betrayers around Roosevelt from prompting the president to injure, even more than he had done, Britain's position in the world.
If any of you will take the trouble to read the book "As He Saw It" by General Elliott Roosevelt, the son of the late president, he will find some very frank statements concerning some of these things. It is apparent that General Elliott Roosevelt was determined to tell the truth so that posterity would have it. He was with his father at Casablanca1, evidently as a military adviser. On page 116 he indicates his father's anti-British attitude in a quotation from what his father said, as follows:
I will work with all my might and main to see to it that the United States is not wheedled into the position of accepting any plan that will aid or abet the British empire in its imperial ambitions.
I remind you that those words were said by Mr. Roosevelt just before he issued his unconditional surrender proclamation on Saturday, January 23, 1943. The next day Mr. Roosevelt again said to his son:
The British must never get the idea that we're in this war just to help them hang on to the archaic medieval empire ideas.
There are many people who interpreted this attitude toward Britain, along with the great delight that Mr. Roosevelt had in making Churchill squirm, as the reason for the president siding with Stalin on the choice of a strategically insignificant area for the Mediterranean front rather than the corridor up through which Mr. Churchill felt it would be comparatively easy to drive into the very heart of nazi territory. Mr. Roosevelt was condemned by those words of his son far more strongly than by anything ever said by my leader.
What was the position of Churchill at Yalta and Teheran? Just because the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) says Mr. Churchill was there and Mr. Eden was there, that does not mean they could not be wrong. Mr. Churchill can be wrong. There is no living individual who is infallible. The hon. member brings in the name of Churchill as if everybody is going to step up and say "hurrah, hurrah". Mr. Churchill can be wrong. Let us also remember that men can be made and men can be broken. Personally I think Mr. Roosevelt was a much overrated man; congenial of course, but the press and the whole propaganda machine of the United States were behind him as they were behind Truman.
What is more, that same propaganda machine can make men and break them. I am not saying whether Mr. Churchill was right or wrong, but I wonder if the hon. member for Kootenay East has ever studied the position of these three big men of the earth as they sat around the table at Teheran and Yalta. Let us look at them. There was Mr. Roosevelt, the president of the United States of America. He was the man who held the purse. There was Mr. Stalin, the man of steel, with a mind as sharp as a two-edged sword and a heart bent on world conquest. There was Mr. Churchill, with one of the greatest burdens of responsibility upon his shoulders, nothing more nor less than the destiny of one of the greatest of peoples of all times, a nation crowded on a small island whose resources were then well spent.
In this connection I do not think I can do much better than quote the remarks of the well-known columnist, George Sokolsky, which appeared in the New York Sun on March 8, 1945. I gather from the article that he covered the meeting at Teheran. What did he say about Churchill? These are his words:
One of these men (the big three) is a British aristocrat, Conservative, imperialistic, proud, the most heroic political figure of the war. But he heads an empire that has long been used to the limit. Its principal resource now is the treasury and industry of the United States. His mind is robust, but his purse is bare. At a bargain he sits with empty hands and high hopes.
That is Mr. Churchill at these conferences. One of my colleagues has passed me a note indicating that I have two minutes left. I can finish in that time because I do not think I need to say anything further. If it is thought that we differ at times with government policy respecting foreign affairs, we want it to be understood that we do so not because we sit on the opposition side of the house and not because we oppose any individual with whom we may disagree, but because we have a conscience and a conviction concerning the destinies of the nations of the world.
