I do not intend to deal very fully with the matter of economic aid. I think that can be done later on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). But there are three or four things which it is my opinion we must do if we are to build the economies of Europe to the point where they can carry the military establishments that they are being asked to carry under NATO.
First, I think we are going to have to purchase more goods from Europe. We are going to have to remove some of the barriers that are in the way of the purchase of these goods in Canada and the United States. Then I think we are going to have to take sterling in exchange for some of the goods we wish to sell to Europe. I believe we shall have to invest that sterling in projects in the sterling area or make loans to the governments of the commonwealth to enable them to develop some of their great natural resources. I believe that if we carried out those two or three things, encouraged private investment and had some public investment or made it easier for the old countries to trade with us, we would overcome that situation.

External Affairs
I want particularly to deal with the latter of the two subjects I mentioned, that is the assistance to underdeveloped areas. When Chief Justice William Douglas of the United States supreme court returned from Asia a year or two ago he said the United States had been so busy fighting against communism that it had not tried to fight against the conditions that breed communism. If that is so in the United States, I think some of the figures I have here will point up the fact that it is even more so in Canada. In his speech the other day at page 1851 of Hansard, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said this, when speaking of the recent commonwealth conference:
The effectiveness of this commonwealth conference cannot, of course, be judged finally until more is known of the measures adopted by individual governments following it, and until further discussions have taken place between its members and other governments, particularly the government of the United States, and with various international organizations, particularly the organization for European economic co-operation. The commonwealth countries have, however, taken a useful initiative. In following it up there will have to be co-operation on the broadest possible basis to ease the necessary but not easy adjustments which may have to be made, especially by some of the members of the commonwealth. In this process the Canadian government will naturally wish to play a full and, I hope, constructive part.
I want to give some figures as to the constructive part the Canadian government has been playing with regard to grants to these areas of the world which need some assistance at this time. I am speaking only of grants, and I shall deal with loans later. During the last four fiscal years, 1949 to 1952, Canada has given in non-military foreign grants a total of $51,765,900, while during the equivalent fiscal years the United States has given $15,817 million in non-military grants. This aid has been given since approximately the beginning of the ECA program in the United States, which started in April, 1948. The Canadian figures, by years, are as follows- I shall not give the odd figures but just the even thousands: In 1949, $5,811,000; 1950, $6,959,000; 1951, $12,313,000; 1952, $26,683,000. In the equivalent years the United States grants have been, 1949, $5,423 million; 1950, $4,620 million; 1951, $3,225 million; 1952, $2,549 million.
Let us take it on a per capita basis; since the United States is a large country and has a much greater population than we have, I think that is the only fair way. On a per capita basis Canada's actual grants during this period were $3.69 while the United States gave, on a per capita basis, $102 or almost 30 times as much as each Canadian. I believe those are rather startling figures. I do not think we in this country have anything

of which to be proud in the grants of economic aid which we have made available to other parts of the world. This economic aid has been given through various organizations such as the Colombo plan, the United Nations technical assistance program, and so on. Canada's total grants for four years should have been $1,237,215,000, if we had been giving on the basis of our productive capacity, rather than the meagre $51,765,900 which we did give.
During those years we in Canada were receiving considerable benefits from those grants given by the United States for assistance to Europe and other parts of the world. Many of our agricultural products and manufactured articles were being sold to Europe and paid for out of grants which the United States was making during this period. Canada benefited under ECA through United States offshore purchases from April, 1947 to March 1952 to the extent of $1,136,700,000. During this time we were giving aid to those countries totalling about $51,765,000 and we were benefiting by over $1,136,000,000 in purchases made out of United States funds. During that period we contributed not one cent to direct European aid. Our position is not very strong, therefore, when the minister suggests that the United States must come in with the commonwealth in providing greater sums of money for economic aid to the various parts of the world.
I have a table here showing contributions Canada has made over the past four years. It shows that under I.R.O. we contributed $5,411,000 in 1949; 1950, $5,826,000;	1951,
$2,107,000. For Near East relief we contributed in 1949, $73,800; in 1950, $57,400; in
1951,	$1,500,000. For post-UNRRA relief we contributed in 1949 about $325,000; under the United Nations expanded program for technical assistance, about $850,000; contribution to United Nations relief and rehabilitation program in Korea, $7,250,000; Colombo plan, $25 million; commonwealth consultative committee on south and southeast Asia, $265,000 in 1952; to provide for purchase and transportation to Yugoslavia of relief supplies in
1952,	$43,800; to provide for gifts of wheat or flour as a contribution to famine relief in Greece, some $825,000.
Those are figures for our direct contributions in the way of grants in aid to these countries during the last four years. In view of the amount we are spending and have been spending in Canada on military preparedness, and the budgetary surpluses we have had in those years in this country, I think the amount we have contributed is a miserable figure to try to build up better conditions in the world and to combat communism.

What did we have by way of budgetary surpluses in those years? In 1949 we had a surplus of $595,500,000; in 1950 we had $131,500,000; in 1951 we had $211,300,000; in 1952 we had $249 million, or a total surplus of $1,187,350,000. During a similar period we could contribute in grants only some $51,765,000 to combat communism in other parts of the world.
Let us now see what we did in some other respects, because we did a great deal more than that. In credits, in military relief, including those grants I have mentioned, and NATO mutual aid, we contributed between 1945 and 1952 some $2,410 million. That is a large sum of money. Let us see what the United States did. During a similar period the United States contributed $35,623 million; and in those contributions I have mentioned that we made during that time, the largest single item was the loan we made to Great Britain just after the war amounting to some $1,250 million. In loans and military aid we were somewhere near in proportion to the amounts given by the United States-[DOT] that is, on a per capita basis-but when it comes to straight grants in aid, we just do not compare with them at all. In other words, the United States have contributed about 30 times as much per capita as have we in Canada.
Let us see what our national defence expenditures were in those years. According to the public accounts, in 1949 we spent $264,820,000; in 1950, $380,948,000; in 1951 $780,204,000; and in 1952, $1,415,473,000. Last year our estimates of expenditure were $2,001 million. This year it is estimated that we will spend approximately the same amount, or another $2 billion. In other words, in the four-year period when we gave $51,765,000 in grants in aid, we spent in military preparedness $2,841 million. I do not think that is a fair proportion or division of the amount of money we in Canada have to spend if we are honest in saying-as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) have said on various occasions-that we shall not be able to accomplish the things we want to accomplish unless we can build up the economies of these backward countries, unless we can assist Europe to establish a sound economy, unless we are prepared to see that these countries have a strong economic background on which to base their military establishments and unless we are prepared to see that in Asia and these other countries some technical assistance is given there, because military preparedness is not enough.
With regard to that matter I should like to quote what the minister said on technical 68108-126
External Affairs
assistance under the Colombo plan. As reported at page 1851 of Hansard he stated:
Another commonwealth initiative on which I can only touch at this time, but which I am sure will be given consideration later, is the Colombo plan, which likewise was framed in full awareness of the interests of other countries and other organizations, particularly the United Nations. That plan is now nearing the end of its second year and it continues to be one of the most important and constructive elements in our foreign economic policy.
When I looked over a release of the United Kingdom information office of December 11, 1952 in connection with the Colombo plan, I was rather surprised to find that there was a branch set up to give technical assistance to those nations of the commonwealth. In this pamphlet we find this statement:
The original members of the council were the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan and Ceylon. They were joined as full members in 1951 by Viet Nam and Cambodia, and early in 1952 by Burma and Nepal.
This council is set up for the purpose of giving technical assistance and of organizing in those various countries places of training for personnel who will go out and assist the inhabitants of those countries in building a better economy. It is stated here:
Co-operation is the key-note of the scheme . . . India has agreed to provide assistance to the value of Rs. 10 million (£750,000) . . .
Pakistan, Ceylon, Indonesia and other countries are putting in similar amounts in order to assist.
Pakistan has offered a contribution of Rs. H million to cover scholarships, fellowships and the provision of experts and training facilities: it has offered Ceylon four scholarships in sugar agronomy and training facilities relating to a projected vegetable oil mill. Ceylon is to contribute Rs. 1,776,000 for each year of the scheme and is providing training facilities in rural development work and the working of co-operatives.
Here is what I was surprised at, when I came to what had been done by the various countries:
As on 31st August, 1952, the services of 80 experts and training facilities for 658 persons had been offered and accepted under the scheme. The allocation of experts was as follows: India-15; Pakistan-36; and Ceylon-29.
Then listen to this:
The supplying countries were the United Kingdom-39; Canada-4; Australia-21; New Zealand- 13; and India-3.
When it comes to supplying facilities for training in the field, this is the situation:
The facilities were provided by the United Kingdom-207; Canada-95; Australia-218; New Zealand -107; India-30 and Pakistan-1.
I do not think we have anything to be proud of in that record; but I want to be fair. I want to point out that Canada, in providing these experts, decided that she would use the

External Affairs
technical assistance program of the United Nations in providing the facilities. In Canada and the United Nations, 1951-52, at page 48, we find this statement:
In an effort to co-ordinate its own participation in the expanded program, Canada sought to obtain the agreement of all the participating organizations to channel their activities in recruiting experts or in placing trainees in Canada through the technical co-operation service which had been set up in the Department of Trade and Commerce. By June 1952 a total of 54 trainees had been sent to Canada by the technical assistance administration for training in fields which included public administration, agriculture, hydroelectric power development and social welfare. These students have come from such countries as India, Pakistan, Cuba, Finland, Brazil, Uruguay, Burma, Venezuela and the British West Indies. By that date 24 experts had been recruited from Canada by the technical assistance administration and the specialized agencies.
If we total up the experts we have placed at the disposal of both these schemes, and if we add the trainees that we have accepted in Canada, some 58 trainees from all of Asia and these other underdeveloped countries, up to June, 1952, it does not seem to me that you get a reasonable contribution on the part of this government to building better technical understanding and better relations with the countries in the Far East and the Near East. It seems to me that, with the facilities we have here in Canada, we should be able to do much more than we have been doing to date in the training of personnel in this country and in the bringing of individuals from these backward countries for training in Canada.
I am convinced that if we are to meet the threat of communism in the world today, the only sensible way to do it is to bring some of the young people from these countries over to Canada, to the United States, to Great Britain and to the other democratic countries and show them what we have here, show them that we have a system that works, that we have a system that provides plenty. If we fail to do it, then make no mistake; Russia is not going to fail to do it. She is not going to fail to take them to her country and give them every opportunity, and try to show them that they have a better system than we have.
In my estimation that is the only way we are going to get value for the amount of money we are spending on military preparedness today. To get value we have to build up the economies of these countries so they can assist themselves. So far I do not think that we in Canada are doing anything like what we can and should do in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, an ordinary backbencher hesitates to participate in a debate dealing with external affairs.
TMr. Wright.]
We are aware of the fact that this particular area of interest involves a very complex field indeed.
As I have sat in this house and listened to debates on various topics I have been encouraged as a backbencher to feel that I might be able to make some small contribution to this discussion, because I find that ability or expert knowledge is not necessarily equated with the length of speeches on any particular topic. As a matter of fact, in a little aside that went on just before I rose to my feet, someone near me expressed the thought that he was not taking part in this debate because he had only one idea on the subject and he did not think that was adequate resources. The rejoinder was that very often this particular person had spoken on a subject with more limited resources than even one idea.
I rise to deal with this topic because actually it is the most important problem that faces hon. members. If we do not solve the difficulties of external affairs, obviously of course we will solve nothing. We are blessed today in Canada, as well as the people in other parts of the western world, with the most incredible material progress that mankind has seen. During the past 200 years the west has passed through a state of progress, so far as material and technical civilization are concerned, that is almost beyond the capacity of the mind to grasp.
In 1750, if we go back that far, if we were to look at the conditions of the peasant in either Europe or Asia, we would find that actually there was very little to distinguish between the two. Today there is absolutely no comparison at all. What is most disconcerting is that we have emerged into the post-war atomic era and we find that the speed of technological change has increased rather than diminished. It has brought western nations to a fundamental crisis which I suppose could be called a moral crisis rather than anything else, in that our moral development and social intelligence have failed to keep pace with our material development.
So far as the sphere of political activity is concerned, we have noted, in the internal situation as well as the external, the tendency toward increased concentration on political power. In the field of external relations we find today, if we were to try to sum up the problem in the simplest terms, two great world powers facing one another and not on very amiable terms. We have the U.S.S.R. and its satellites on one hand, the eastern group; and in the other, the western group, we have

the United States of America and her associates. I use the term "satellite" and "associates" to distinguish the relationship that exists between the Soviet and those within her sphere of influence, and the United States of America and the countries which come within her orbit of influence.
Actually, either of those world powers- and they are just that, world powers-could exercise world control without any difficulty at all, were it not for the existence of the other. We have the means of communication and transportation, as a result of developments on the scientific and material levels, that would make it possible for either of those powers to achieve in concrete political terms what has been the overwhelming desire of world powers from the beginning of the history of mankind. Therefore when the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) makes reference to the positive attitude of this group toward the United States of America, I do not think he can infer that we have necessarily allowed ourselves to be completely dominated, to come completely under the control of that particular sphere of influence. I think actually the situation is the result of political reality. Whether we like it or not, the United States of America is leading the western nations in the struggle for world domination between communism and the western democracies.
What is most difficult in this problem is the fact that today, in dealing with political matters, we are faced with the threat of atomic warfare. In listening to Mr. Truman give his last statement to Congress before he retired from the presidency of the United States, I was interested in a particular point. He said something like this, and he addressed his remarks directly to Stalin. I do not know whether that gentleman was listening, but Mr. Truman intended the remarks for Stalin's ears. He said:
You claim belief in Lenin's prophecy that one stage in the development of communist society would be war between your world and ours. But Lenin was a pre-atomic man who viewed society and history with pre-atomic eyes. Something profound has happened since he wrote. War has changed its shape and dimensions. It cannot be a stage in the development of anything save ruin.
I am sure hon. members in this chamber will agree with these words of the former president of the United States that today war can mean only inevitable ruin for civilization. We have within our grasp the power to incinerate fifty million people within a space of five minutes, if it ever happens that the hot war should break out in full intensity.
It is because of this that I feel the present debate is of the utmost importance and, as a backbencher, I am going to make 68108-126J
External Affairs
some small contribution to the discussion. The interest aroused from this debate, as the various points are discussed in the chamber and in the press, will create in the minds of the public an awareness of the gravity of the situation.
It seems to me that in Canada we have been more preoccupied with our own material development and prosperity than in acknowledging our obligations, as we are confronted with this extremely grave external situation. I suppose politicians-not necessarily those on the opposition side-have been more at fault than others for having stirred up a false sense of well-being and security, and for having harped constantly on the theme of Canadian prosperity. Our prosperity is meaningless if we do not do something to solve the very difficult problem that, as an autonomous nation within the framework of the British commonwealth, we are forced to face.
My thinking on the matter has been shaped largely outside this chamber. I have not had the opportunity to sit through many debates on external affairs during my membership in the house. Many of the ideas I shall bring forth were formulated in the weird and wonderful period immediately following world war II. Those of us who served in that war were deeply interested in what was then popularly described as the winning of the peace. It was said that a military victory was useless unless we were equally successful in winning the peace. Everyone was heartened as we saw the United Nations take shape to deal with problems affecting international relations.
Unfortunately, as has been indicated by several speakers in this debate, the United Nations got bogged down in fuzzy idealism. After the second world war we believed, as we did after world war I, that the world had been made safe for democracy. The original claim of the United Nations, unfortunately, has not been realized in actuality. I do not believe there was anything sinister in connection with what happened when the United Nations was formed. Actually, as I have already pointed out, the same attitude prevailed at the time of the formation of the league of nations after world war I. I do not think there was any world conspiracy that dominated that organization. Rather it was apathy, lack of interest, lack of understanding and comprehension on the part of those who were responsible for guiding the affairs of the world.
For example I believe it was President Harding who refused even to acknowledge communications from the league of nations, and it was such apathy, lack of interest and

External Affairs
isolationism that sabotaged that organization. I do not think there is anything sinister in what occurred in respect of the league of nations. It was a matter of indifference; and perhaps during the twentieth century ideas emerged preventing the real issues from being faced by those who were most responsible for carrying out the early negotiations of that international body.
Today, as the result of failure by the United Nations to grapple successfully with the problem of winning the peace, we find ourselves in a cold war period. In this changed situation the borderline between peace and war has become somewhat blurred. When the house commenced its deliberations this afternoon, for example, an effort was made, through a question asked in the house, to ascertain whether or not we are now actually engaged in war.
While we were indulging in wishful thinking the Russians, true to form-and had we had any knowledge of history we would have expected it-seized	the initiative and
succeeded in building up a buffer of "friendly" satellites. This was done with very little effort on the part of Russia. At that time the west had neither the power nor the will to resist. Actually, if we had had an understanding of the communist world movement we should have been aware that this condition of affairs would have developed; because communism, as an ideology, must be recognized as a world religion. One of the strong motivating factors in the communist idea is the religious faith it arouses in its devotees. It appears to have great strength in areas where there is a religious vacuum; and we know there are many religious vacuums around the world today.
In addition to the religious aspect of communism it is utterly and absolutely opposed to what is sometimes described as western capitalism. It has as its fundamental objective the extermination in any way possible of the capitalist form of society. Communism has its imperialistic aspect. For example, it is significant that the only countries that have been brought within the scope of soviet influence by internal disorder have been China and Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia is now afflicted with an interesting disease called Titoism, and it is hoped that China, that vast and mysterious country of the east, will become afflicted with the same political illness. It seems inconceivable that China will allow herself to remain indefinitely the puppet of the political manipulators in Moscow. An understanding of the true nature of Russian communism, as well as its religious and imperialistic aspects, should have put us on the alert, so far as the post-war activities of that nation are concerned. Instead of
that, both at Yalta and at Potsdam, as has been indicated in this debate, we took the attitude of compromise and conciliation, an attitude similar to that taken toward the nazis before world war II. At that time the slogan was: Let's not be nasty to the nazis. This time it was: Let's not be nasty to the soviets. We indulged in wholesale disarmament while Russia, very easily and without much effort on her part, was gobbling up the countries within her immediate sphere of influence. And it is only recently, since the reorganization of the cominform in 1947, that we have begun to stiffen our attitude toward communist imperialism.
Today we have the soviets at bay in the west since the formation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It is rather an encouraging sign that since NATO was established there has been every evidence cf increasing solidarity in western European countries. It is almost possible to conclude that the situation, so far as Europe is concerned, has been stabilized because at long last the western powers have awakened to the reality of Russian intent and they are offering firm resistance to any further encroachment by that world power.
Today Russia has been stopped temporarily in the west. I think the reason she has been stopped is because she realizes that she can make further gains in Europe only at the risk of open conflict. Surely responsible leaders in Russia are no more happy about the prospect of atomic warfare than are we in the west. She came very close to absorbing France and Italy within her sphere of influence. I repeat that we owe much of the relative stability in western Europe today to the wisdom of those who were responsible for promoting the NATO plan.
The question is, can it last? The communist plan is a fluid and mobile one. It was General Eisenhower, when in charge of the European army, who said that Europe cannot be defended unless she unites. Now that General Eisenhower has become president of the United States I imagine he still holds that viewpoint in connection with international affairs and is still of the opinion that we cannot defend Europe against further Russian encroachment unless Europe does unite. I think that could account for the recent statements by the secretary of state, Mr. Dulles, in Europe, when he emphasized the necessity of European union in order to preserve the situation as it stands at the moment.
So much for Europe. I have listened to this discussion with a great deal of interest, and have realized that Europe and NATO have been considerably in the background.

Our attention has been focused upon east Asian matters precipitated by the recent announcement concerning Formosa. I do not think we can call what is taking place in east Asia a cold war. The term "cold war" as I have indicated suggests a blurred understanding of what is actually peace and what is war. The minister of external affairs has referred to Korea as a police action. As I read the reports from that area and try to keep in touch with the situation it seems to me to be a pretty hot police action, almost hot enough to be called a hot war.
Unfortunately the situation in Asia is not turning out as well as it has in western Europe. The situation in Asia as represented by the stalemate in Korea is weighing heavily against the democracies. It is a very delicate situation indeed, because there we have not the background of democratic traditions and type of thinking that we found in the west which made it possible for the western powers to come together once they were made aware of the imperialistic drive of communism.
In Asia it is more than a case of communism versus democracy. In the eastern part of the world we have been witnessing during recent years, ever since the west became interested in the Orient as a matter of fact, the beginning of an industrial revolution with its consequent effects upon nationalism and racialism. What is taking place in Indo-China, Indonesia, Malaya and throughout the east, and also to a certain extent in China, is the result primarily of influences that have come in from the west.
The missionaries who have gone there have preached the fundamental ideas of Christianity, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Those ideas have had a tremendous impact upon the Asian people. Not only have we sent religious missionaries; we have sent political prophets who have expounded the principles of freedom and liberty to people who have no background of democratic thought or experience. Then our commercial salesmen followed in the wake of the missionaries and introduced the peoples of the east, who I suppose were at a stage of economic development which could be compared to that existing in Europe some four or five hundred years ago, to the material benefits of our western way of life.
It seems to me that the real difficulty in the east arises from nationalistic sentiments. I think it is obvious to those who are familiar with the situation that the events that have been taking place in China over some decades, but more recently since world war II, are interpreted by the people of east Asia as a triumph of Asiatic nationalism
External Affairs
over what they call western colonial oppression, and it is very easy for Russia to sell that notion to the Chinese people. The people of the east are very suspicious of the motives of the western nations as they endeavour to stabilize an extremely difficult situation in that part of the world. I suppose they have cause to be suspicious, because it is not so many years ago that the western powers were carrying on what might be termed colonial oppression.
The crux of the matter, as I see it, in east Asia is what is going to happen to the 800 million people who are still outside the orbit of soviet influence. They are being weighed in the balance at the moment. We do not know whether they are going to move in the direction of the western democracies or be inveigled by the false promises of liberty and economic benefits which Russia and communism can hold out before the eyes of these people. We have found that communism is capable of being all things to all people until it actually takes over and is in political control of the situation. That seems to be the crux of the matter. What happens in regard to the east as negotiations are carried on at the United Nations is going to determine very largely the direction in which the people will turn.
So far as China is concerned, it used to be thought that the social and political revolution that has occurred in that country was merely a continuation of the agrarian reform movement that has been going on for a long time in that country. But today, as we see the participation of the Chinese communists in Korea, we cannot fail to recognize that behind that effort is the subtle manipulation of the Soviets. We are faced with a situation very similar to that which confronted us shortly after world war II. The pressure that was formerly exerted on the satellite countries of Europe is now being exerted in Korea; and as I have indicated, the situation has been exploited very favourably by the Soviets thus far on their own behalf.
If it is true in the east, as it was in the west, that the Soviets only understand a firm voice, I do not think we need become too disturbed and this is an opinion that has already been expressed by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) about the recent United States action with respect to Formosa, because to me it merely seems to indicate that the pressure that was applied in the west is now going to be applied in the east. We must remember, of course, that there is greater danger of open conflict in the Asiatic situation because of the nationalism and

External Affairs
racialism and the social and political upheaval I have briefly outlined. However, inasmuch as Russia responded to increased pressure in the west, why should she not react in the same manner to increased pressure in the Asian sphere of influence? A firm voice in the west brought results. If Russia shows the same reluctance to face an outbreak of hostilities that she did in the west, surely she will be reasonable enougn to withdraw from a situation that could be made untenable once the western powers indicate their real intent there.
We must always remember, of course-and this is a difficulty no one can resolve-that no one can decide what Russia is going to do. Actually the answer is in her hands, and it might be that with madmen in authority she will precipitate the world into the ruinous war, a war that everyone fervently hopes will never occur, because it is a foregone conclusion in this atomic age that war can only result in ruin for all the peoples of the world.
It has been suggested by this group that a positive contribution toward the stabilization of the situation in Asia might be made by the creation of a pact or organization similar to that which was established in western Europe. The minister has been reluctant to meet the situation head on with a pointblank statement. We have been faced with embarrassing unilateral action on the part of the United States. Much of the discussion that has gone on in the house has been of a speculative variety concerning the true intent of that country, whether they are going to push the struggle in the east right to the limit, which means open warfare, or whether their action merely reflects a stiffening resistance. Apparently we do not know, mainly because we were not consulted.
It seems to me that the success achieved by NATO in stabilizing the European situation might also be realized in the east if we were able to get together in some form of Pacific pact or organization. In order to avoid the possibility of armed conflict, certainly everything in our power must be done. If a Pacific pact can help, it seems to me it would be a logical step in proceeding toward some form of political machinery for resolving by negotiation and agreement the difficulty that exists between the two world powers, these two gigantic spheres of influence, the U.S.S.R. on the one side and the United States on the other. As to the question of who shall join such a Pacific pact, that would resolve itself as the organization took shape, just as it has in the case of

NATO which now extends its sphere of influence far beyond the immediate geographic area of the Atlantic.
In the immediate post-war period after world war II we talked about winning the peace, we talked about one world or none. The slogan "one world or none" is just as applicable now as it was in those days. The United Nations must succeed. It is the ultimate hope for carrying on international negotiations by peaceful means. At the moment it is blocked because of the difficulty that has arisen between the eastern and western spheres of influence. We must work toward the establishment of some form of political machinery whereby international affairs can be settled by discussion and agreement and not by participation in a devastating war.
I say again that here is the heart of the matter. It is essentially a moral problem. Because of the rapid rate of scientific and materialistic progress we have been precipitated violently into a world in which we have neither the social intelligence nor the moral integrity to handle the problems that have developed. That gap must be bridged if humanity is to survive.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate on external affairs until I saw in the press this morning that the debate was to be concluded today. Therefore I thought I should like to make a few observations at this time. It seems to me that this is a great day for the backbenchers, because they are taking part in the debate at the present time.
First of all I want to extend my congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on being chosen president of the seventh session of the general assembly of the United Nations. It is a great tribute to him in his own right and a gesture of good will to Canada as well. I am sure that he will preside at the meetings of the assembly with firmness and efficiency that will bring credit, as has always been the case at external affairs meetings, not only to himself but to the great dominion which he so ably represents.
I am not going to take much time to debate the different problems that confront us in respect to external affairs. I am not going to talk about the great problems confronting NATO, or the problems of the Near East and Middle East, great as they are, because they have already been discussed by members of the house who are much better qualified to do so than I am. I do not profess to be an expert or even an authority on external

affairs, because it does seem to me that is a line of study that is available to very few people.
I do want to make some reference to the situation in the Far East and the recent change in policy made by President Eisenhower, which has caused a great deal of consternation throughout the world because of the fear that the government of the United States may take further action in this regard which, without bringing to an end the war in Korea, could easily develop into a third global war.
In referring to that, I should like to quote briefly from an editorial that appeared a few ' days ago in the Citizen which I felt summarized the matter very well. It reads:
Reassuring statements in Washington have as yet only partially allayed British and west European alarm at President Eisenhower's decision to end the "neutralization" of Formosa. The disturbing fact is that unilateral action by the United States in the Far East cannot be kept separate from United Nations action in Korea. For Canada, with its American, commonwealth, and U.N. links, the situation is particularly difficult. But now is the time to take a stand, and in parliament on Wednesday the external affairs minister, Mr. Pearson, made plain that Canadian exertions in Korea are for no other cause than that of the United Nations.
The complicating factor is United States foreign policy, which has been developed at the same time as the Americans have given the U.N. leadership in Korea. Regarding the Chinese communist victory as defeat for that policy, some Americans have continued to hope that the restoration of Chiang Kai-shek's regime, now on Formosa, might be engineered or assisted. So the Truman administration simultaneously rallied the U.N. to defend South Korea and sent a fleet to protect Formosa, lest the mainland Chinese should think the situation ripe for an attempt to conclude the civil war by an attack on Chiang Kai-shek.
The United States alone preserved and built up Chiang's forces, while not preventing them from making minor raids on the mainland. It has now released them for any larger enterprises that may be considered feasible, and has promised increased aid. The theory is that China may be forced to come to terms in Korea. But this policy plays into the hands of those in the west who want the western nations to try to reverse the Chinese revolution, and indeed to achieve the effective restoration of their former power throughout most of Asia. It would be likely to consolidate communist Asia, Russian and Chinese, since antiwestern feeling has contributed powerfully to communist success. It would alienate non-communist Asia, where suspicion of the west is still strong. The spread of fighting might result in a major war.
Mr. Pearson has very likely foreseen all these dangers. He has reiterated the Canadian government's view that the concern of the United Nations is not to intervene in Chinese affairs, not to spread the hostilities, but only to protect South Korea. This position is likely to commend itself to parliament.
I was in New York early in December, and while not there as an official delegate of Canada I spent several days at the United
External Affairs
Nations assembly and attended political committee meetings from time to time. When the Indian plan was presented as a means of ending the Korean conflict I hoped that this would be accepted by the Russian delegates and their satellite nations, who were the spokesmen for the Chinese and North Koreans on that occasion. Since this was an Asian plan and was promoted by a free state, it could not in any sense of the word be considered as an imperialist plot. I felt that it would surely be accepted. But after listening to the spokesman for the Russian delegation, Mr. Vishinsky, in his tirade against this plan, I knew that it would not be accepted.
The plan represented a compromise safeguarding the principle of non-forcible repatriation of war prisoners, while conceding to the Chinese the right to have representatives from two communistic countries on the screening committee. The rejection has made a negotiated peace much more difficult than ever to achieve, and has increased the danger of the Korean conflict spreading. Undoubtedly this change in policy by the United States was designed to relieve the pressure on the Korean front which could, in turn, convince the North Korean and Chinese communists that the stalemate in Korea could not continue much longer, and that peace would be much more desirable. This action on the part of President Eisenhower would seem to eliminate all the provisions of the Cairo agreement that was signed in 1943 by Churchill, Roosevelt and Chiang Kai-shek, the leader of the nationalist government.
Under the terms of that agreement, Formosa was to be returned to the Chinese republic after the cessation of hostilities. The situation is most difficult because the United States still recognizes the nationalist government that operates from Formosa as the government of China, yet Great Britain, whose government is still headed by the same man who signed the Cairo agreement, recognizes the new communist regime. The United States policy can only be interpreted as one that allows the nationalist government to carry on its operations against the mainland, and also assists it with arms, war munitions and material. At the same time the seventh fleet could be used to protect Formosa from any attack from the mainland of China. This could lead to a global or third world war which, if at all possible, we want to avoid.
On former occasions I have spoken in this house regarding the situation in China. I do not think it would serve any useful purpose to thresh old straw. I do not believe it would accomplish much to go over the merits or

External Affairs
demerits of the former regime in China, because I believe they have been well established in the world at large. I do believe there are a few basic facts that should be pointed out. In reading Hansard of Friday night, I believe it was, I noticed that the member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), in speaking of the nationalist government of China, said they had the same ideas we have. This afternoon I was amazed to hear some members state that the late Franklin Roosevelt was a much overrated man. Personally I was a great admirer of the late Franklin D. Roosevelt. I recall the occasion upon which he visited this parliament, and one of the things that was a revelation to me was that a man who had such a physical handicap would carry on in the service of his country and make such contributions to his fellow men during his lifetime.
As I said, I was a great admirer of the late Franklin D. Roosevelt. One of the things that impressed me was the statement he issued regarding the four freedoms of our democracy, freedoms of which he was the champion and the director. The first of these was the freedom of speech and assembly. The second was the freedom of worship. I was in China for almost two and a half years, and I would say that freedom of worship was in evidence all over China. In Shanghai there were many, many churches. I remember that in the old French concession, in what we called the Zeg Wai district, the Catholic church had a very large organization. They had schools for boys and for girls; they had a nursery started. We went there many times because we, as a relief and rehabilitation organization, on many occasions had given them relief supplies in the nature of clothing and flour.
I visited the cathedral there. Next to Notre Dame cathedral in Montreal and one in New York, I think it was the greatest cathedral I was ever in. There was freedom of worship in all of the different communities throughout the city. They worshipped there as they cared to. In the community centre, which was part of the old American zone, the community church was there, and I used to attend the community church service. When there one Sunday-and I am sure my friend the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) would be interested in this-I heard the late ambassador to China, Leighton Stuart, make an extremely fine address. I think that was in July, 1947. Today the local temples are, I believe, still open for worship as they were on former occasions; but the missions and the churches that have been conducted by
[Mr. MacKenzie.l
the people of foreign districts or of foreign lands do not enjoy the freedom of worship they had when I was there.
Of course this question about the nationalist government and its merits or demerits is something that was a political question in the United States. As a matter of fact, during the last presidential election the matter was discussed at some length and people took both sides, and did so rather heatedly. There were honest opinions expressed, I have no doubt, on both sides, and that was their right. But when we think about these names that have been prominent in China for so many years:	T.
V. Soong; Dr. T. F. Tsiang; Dr. H. H. Kung; K. C. Wu and General Claire Chennault, many of them recall old acquaintances that I had when I was in that Far East country. Mr. Wu was at that time mayor of the city of Shanghai. He did a good job. He is now the governor of Formosa. It is unfortunate that he was not there in the first place, because he probably could have avoided that most disastrous massacre of the people which was conducted by the former governor.
As to Major General Chennault, I met him on several occasions, and had the privilege and pleasure of meeting him one night and entertaining him in one of the hotel rooms. He was at that time the president of the civil air transport, CAT. He was doing quite a large commercial business there. They eventually amalgamated with another commercial air line, and they had almost a monopoly on the commercial air lines in China.
When the generalissimo took over the Chinese republic, the first president of the executive council and practically the premier was T. V. Soong. In 1928 he took over, and he held that position until 1933 when H. H. Kung replaced him. Both these men, by the way, were brothers-in-law of the president. He was kept in power until 1944, when Soong was again re-established as president and premier of the Chinese republic.
When I arrived in China in 1945 T. V. Soong was the president of the executive union and also the premier. We distributed a great'many relief supplies to the Chinese people. T. V. Soong at that time was the man actually in charge. He tried, to some extent, to control the provisions that were sent over under the United Nations relief and rehabilitation program. I well remember that in 1946, when 550,000 bales of cotton were distributed in China in order to rehabilitate the industry and also to provide relief clothing, 75 per cent of that cotton was distributed among Chinese-owned mills

which were actually T. V. Soong and company's mills; because they took over the former Japanese mills in Shanghai and operated them under the name of C.T.I.I. or China Textile Industries Incorporated. They made much of that cotton into uniforms for the armed services. Of course that was completely contrary to the terms of the contract that was made for the distribution of those supplies.
The director of the CNRRA organization which, after all, was under the control of T. V. Soong, was Dr. T. F. Tsiang. I have not my records here so that I can be exact, but during that period a protest was sent to Washington in order to stop the supplies coming into China until there was some clarification of where they were to go. These were held back for some time, but later they were released.
Most people now admit that any amount of aid sent to the Chinese nationalist forces when they were in power could not have saved them. Mr. Acheson said in a press release that from 1945 to 1951, I think it was, some $2 billion or more of aid was authorized to go to the Chinese republic. Those supplies positively, in many cases, were sold. Whole regiments that were equipped with United States equipment went over to the communists of that time, so that the supplies the United States shipped over at that time played as large if not a larger part in the overthrow of the nationalist government than did the supplies they received from Russia, though Russia unquestionably gave them supplies.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing some of the reasons why, in my opinion, we had lost China as an ally. As a matter of fact, during the first year of the Korean war much of the equipment captured by the allies from the North Koreans was of United States manufacture. It is generally agreed by those who look at this in a realistic way that the war in China could never have been won unless the United States had taken an active part in it and had complete control of all the supplies and equipment they sent in there from time to time.
The question is asked, is the situation much better today? Toward the latter part of 1949 Madame Chiang came to the United
External Affairs
States. On January 8, 1950 she gave a farewell broadcast from New York, and I was fortunate enough to hear it. That night she was very critical of the position Great Britain had taken. She definitely intimated that the recognition of the communist government was of a mercenary nature; that that was what led Great Britain to recognize the new regime in China. She mentioned the fact that Great Britain had possession of Hong Kong and other places that meant so much to her. But she forgot to mention that many of the Asiatic countries had also recognized the new regime. She forgot to mention that many European countries such as Holland, Denmark, Switzerland and Sweden could hardly be regarded as communist countries, and they had recognized the new regime in China.
In 1950 I went to Lake Success; and when I went to the security council and saw the delegates there in their permanent seats I was. actually surprised to find as China's permanent delegate my old friend Dr. T. F. Tsiang whom I knew so well in China and with whom I had quite a few differences in regard to the distribution of materials among the war-devastated and war-ravaged areas of China. According to our contract these supplies were to have been distributed without discrimination as to race, creed or political differences, but of course that is something they just did not do.
If China had been recognized at that time the question is often asked would the situation be any better, would the conditions be any better than they are now. That is a question no one can answer. It is futile even to prophesy as to what would have happened. But I will say this. I do not see how it could have been any worse, at any rate. By recognizing the government of China you would not be approving or disapproving the type of government they had. You would be only acknowledging a fact that already existed. You would be acknowledging that they had restored some order and that they had control of the situation, and that is all that would have been implied in recognition of the government.
I remember sitting in the delegates lounge during 1950 and talking to some of the United States delegates. They said: "Of course we would not recognize a gangster mob. That is something we will not do. How do you expect us to recognize a revolutionary gangster mob?" I remember exactly what they said. They said: "Why these people are in the A1 Capone and Frank Costello class." I said: "I quite appreciate that, but don't forget that in 1917 the Russians had probably one of the cruelest revolutions of all time, in which they liquidated their rulers and took

External Affairs
their property. It was one of the wickedest in all history; still you have recognized them for the last 17 years; you are in full diplomatic relations with them." The fact is, if you go back into history you will find that Chiang himself came into power in the same way. That was hardly a good enough reason for not recognizing China.
What is the situation today? When I was in New York in December I made some inquiries about my old friends whom I knew in China. They probably would not recognize me. As a matter of fact I never met Dr. Kung, but I did meet T. V. Soong. He was a very charming personality. I made inquiries about where they were and what they were doing. I was told that they were settled down in New York. They are pretty well established there. As a matter of fact they are very wealthy. They told me too that Madame Chiang was still there, although I have no proof for that statement. The two brothers-in-law of Chiang, T. V. Soong and Dr. Kung, have become very wealthy, because for a long time they were not only premier and minister of finance of the country, which is a great combination, but they did have a tremendous amount of money. They are conducting and directing one of the most powerful lobbies that has ever taken place in the United States not only in Washington but at the United Nations as well.
I hold in my hand a magazine that is published in New York called the Reporter.
magazine can be obtained in the reading room. In the issues of April 15, 1952 and April 29, 1952 you will find described the most powerful lobby that has taken place in many, many years. They know that the old regime cannot possibly be reinstated in the Chinese homeland unless there is all-out revolution, unless there is a war. That is the only hope they have of being reinstated in their former status. I noticed that in the political committee, when the final vote came on the Indian proposal for peace in Korea, the Chinese delegate abstained from voting.
There are very few of us who fully appreciate that communism in some of these underprivileged and backward countries has a much greater appeal than it has to the people of Canada. I venture to say there is no one in this chamber this evening who knows very much about the pangs of hunger, who knows the devastating effects that hunger and want and privation have on a people. But those people know. And of course communism has a great appeal to them because it promises them a better way of life. It promises to free them from their economic chains. It promises to give them a better
[Mr. MacKenzie.l
standard of living. Naturally, with nothing to lose, they take a chance on it. They do not appreciate that the first objective of communist doctrine is for the state to get complete control of the individual. The second objective is to obtain complete domination over all the people.
In the final analysis the object of communism is world power, bringing with it concentration camps and slave labour. That is something these underprivileged people have not yet realized. Has that stage yet arrived in China? I do not think so, and I believe that with the help of the United Nations that old land may possibly be reinstated.
So in conclusion I ask this question. Do the peoples of the free world want to win China from Russian domination? The answer obviously is yes, that it must be done. Surely we can find some champion of our way of life, our Christian democracy, among the Chinese people, without trying to reinstate the old regime which, in my opinion, will never bring about that condition. Because, eventually, China will break from Russia.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in the debate tonight to support what has been said by hon. members of this group who have already spoken. We are interested chiefly in the situation in Korea, in doing everything possible to prevent an extension of the war and in doing everything possible toward bringing it to a speedy end.
I believe the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) made an excellent contribution to the debate when, among other things, he pointed out what Canada could do by way of economic assistance to Asian countries in order to promote good will and democratic principles in those areas.
I was not able to be in the house on the days the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made his survey of international affairs. However, I read his speeches on both days and, in the main, I believe I can agree with what he said. I felt, however, when reading his speeches, that he should have taken a firmer stand in regard to the Eisenhower instruction to remove the seventh fleet shield from the Chinese mainland.
I gained the impression from reading the minister's speech that he was sitting on the fence, but leaning toward the position taken later by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). We in this group certainly view with alarm the recent order by President Eisenhower in regard to the seventh fleet. Not only do we feel that it was a mistake

but, in common with other members in the house, we have seen statements by other prominent Americans suggesting such things as a naval blockade of the Chinese mainland, air and naval support for Chiang Kai-shek, and the use of new weapons. We are fearful lest this first action by President Eisenhower be followed by actions of the kind I have just mentioned that might, in fact, extend the war to the point where we would be definitely involved in a war on the Asian continent.
We are certainly opposed to any such further steps as might lead to that terrible result. We feel President Eisenhower's order was a mistake, not only because we do not agree with it but because, as we understand it, it was arrived at after very little consultation with the other members of the United Nations involved in the current police action.
I do not think the United States can support United Nations action in Korea and say, on the one hand, that it is the action of the United Nations, and on the other hand feel free in some other way to take unilateral action connected with the Korean conflict. Either the action in Korea is a United Nations action or it is not; and so long as it is a United Nations action we feel that any decision should be taken only after consultation among the nations involved and after general agreement has been achieved.
In the United Kingdom, for example, both the Labour party and the Conservative government are opposed to the recent United States action. I see in a Canadian Press dispatch from London appearing in the Regina Leader-Post of February 3, the following:
Foreign Secretary Eden said Tuesday Britain feels the United States decision on Formosa will have "unfortunate political repercussions without compensating military advantages".
I have seen press reports of the debate that took place at Westminster. Certainly the Labour party is opposed to the Eisenhower directive and feels that it is fraught with the greatest danger. It has been suggested by prominent people in the United States that there should be a blockade of the Chinese mainland. When the blockade was being discussed in the United Kingdom parliament Mr. Herbert Morrison asked a number of questions of Mr. Eden. He asked what the United Kingdom government would do if Chiang Kai-shek, in a blockade he might undertake, interfered with British ships. And he asked this question:
Supposing forces of Chiang Kai-shek conducted a blockade against the Chinese mainland and interfered with British merchant shipping peacefully
External Affairs
going about its business? I would like to ask the foreign secretary to inform us what Her Majesty's government would do. What does the Royal Navy do?
And again:
Replying to that part of the speech, Eden later said "Her Majesty's ships on their lawful occasion would always be protected-that is the duty of any government of this country."
We sincerely hope that such protection by the United Kingdom of British merchant ships will not be necessary, but the discussion in the British House of Commons demonstrates how serious is the United States action and the great danger that is involved.
I think it is important for us in the western world to cultivate the friendship of noncommunist Asian countries such as India and Pakistan. I think it is particularly important that we co-operate with India, and any action by the western world that is opposed by India should be taken only after the most serious consideration. Here we have United States unilateral action which is opposed by the government of India. The Montreal Gazette of February 12 contained a dispatch from New Delhi, as follows:
The Indian government views with "grave concern" the recent developments in the Far East following the United States government's withdrawal of the seventh fleet, President Rajendra Prasad said today in an address to a joint session of parliament.
And the concluding sentence in the dispatch reads:
The address made it clear that Prime Minister Nehru's government totally disapproved of Washington's decision.
I think we are all anxious to have the war in Korea settled. I think we are all anxious that it should not be extended, and I think we should give more regard to the views of the governments of India and the other Asian nations in the free world.
I listened to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie). Because of his experience he is better qualified than I to comment on the Chiang Kai-shek regime, either as it existed on the Chinese mainland or as it presently exists on Formosa. I noticed that he referred to the China lobby in Washington and the people associated with it as the same old crowd. He went on to say that Chiang Kai-shek and the same old crowd could not be reinstated as the government of China without an all-out global war. That is certainly my view. I feel that anything done to reinstate Chiang Kai-shek in China is not only impractical and probably impossible, but would mean the loss of support and good will among other Asian countries.
I have referred to statements by United States leaders. I should like to quote from a

External Affairs
special dispatch to the New York Times, dated Washington, February 8, from Clayton Knowles as follows:
Senator Robert A. Taft of Ohio, Republican leader of the Senate, added fuel today to the major foreign policy debate, now shaping up in Congress, by declaring that the United States already was "at full war" with communist China.
For this reason, he asserted, neither the bombing of Manchurian supply bases north of Korea nor a blockade of the China mainland could be expected to extend the war.
He said he thought a blockade was "desirable" if it could be worked out "without too great international complications with our allies."
There it is. Senator Taft, the Republican leader in the United States Senate, is advocating a blockade of the Chinese mainland and saying that the United States is already at full war with communist China. There is another dispatch in the New York Times of February 8 as follows:
Senator William F. Knowland of California, chairman of the Senate Republican policy committee, said today the United States, alone if necessary, should blockade communist China to increase allied pressure for Korean peace.
And again:
"We should have the co-operation of the British and French in a blockade," Senator Knowland said.
And again:
But if such co-operation is not forthcoming I think we could carry on a unilateral blockade.
I listened to a radio news report last night which said that Senator Knowland had just been on a television broadcast and had reiterated his demand for a blockade of the China coast. We in the C.C.F. are opposed to such blockade because we are afraid it would lead to an extension of the war; we feel that it is impracticable unless shipping could be prevented from reaching the Russian port of Vladivostok because unless that were done commodities would still arrive on the Chinese mainland. Moreover, any such unilateral action by the United States would be disastrous to United Nations action in Korea and would involve us in a global war.
The statement of the minister of external affairs in regard to this matter was certainly very mild, and perhaps because of that we find the following report in the Ottawa Citizen of February 11, in a Reuters news agency item headed "Rely on Canada for Realism" and reading:
The Washington Post says today the United States can usually rely on Canada for realism in foreign affairs as well as plain speaking when the occasion demands it.
It is significant that President Eisenhower's state of the union message, particularly the passage on Formosa, aroused in Canada little of the uneasiness reported from parts of Europe, it adds in a leading article.

I think it would have been much better if the minister of external affairs had taken a stronger stand which could not be interpreted in Washington as indicating that Canada, which is said to usually take a realistic stand, is not greatly alarmed at the action taken. I have noticed other references by the minister of external affairs in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway, and I have heard him speak in regard to United States trade barriers. I congratulate the minister upon the statement he made in reference to the St. Lawrence seaway. Certainly he was telling the United States in firm language that Canada wanted the St. Lawrence seaway and did not want any further stalling on that project. For example, he said:
There is one matter, however, in which our American friends have not been able to co-operate with us at the pace we feel the requirements of the situation demand.
And again:
We hope that it will be soon, and we are disappointed that that decision has not already been reached.
And again:
It has been made clear, however, that the discussion of any new proposal for sharing this task must not delay any longer the whole project.
Other members of the government, such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), have made strong statements from time to time in regard to the desirability of the United States reducing trade barriers. The government are prepared to talk up to the United States when it comes to the St. Lawrence seaway development and international trade, and for that I compliment them. In his speech the other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke with the voice of a lion when dealing with the subject of the St. Lawrence seaway, but when he came to refer to the action that had been taken in connection with Formosa I am afraid that he spoke with the voice of a lamb.
We would like to see him take just as firm a stand with regard to the Formosa action as he has taken with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway. I feel that it is not so easy for the nations in Europe to talk to the United States in the same kind of firm language that Canada could use because these countries have depended, and depend today, on economic assistance from the United States. They are still suffering from the ravages of the recent war, and therefore they need United States economic help.
We in Canada are living in a wealthy country. We do not need to seek economic assistance from the United States. It is true that we are dependent on American good will to a large extent so far as economic and

trade matters are concerned, but the same thing can be said about the United States in relation to Canada. The United States is dependent on Canada for a great many natural products for its own prosperity and well-being. Because Canada is less dependent in its relationship to the United States from an economic standpoint, I think Canada is in the best position of any nation in the world to make her views clear to that country. We are of course a member of the commonwealth; since other members of the commonwealth disagree with the United States policy, and since we are a North American nation, I think we are in a particularly good position to help present their viewpoint to the government of the United States.
I understand that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was in Washington over the week end. I have no doubt that he will be reporting to parliament on his discussions, perhaps this evening. He shakes his head to the contrary. I hope that in his discussions in the United States he has made the Canadian position perfectly clear, and I hope that it is a firmer position but along the lines referred to in the statement he made to the house. If his reception in Washington has not been entirely satisfactory, then I think he should consider one further step. The Prime Minister of Great Britain made a trip to Washington earlier this year to present his views to the President of the United States and exchange views with him. According to an article in the Christian Science Monitor, Mr. Anthony Eden will make a trip to Washington soon, as will Premier Mayer of France.
In order to underline the Canadian position, which I understand is that nothing should be done that might extend the conflict in Korea to other areas, and in order to make that position abundantly clear to the United States, the Secretary of State for External Affairs might recommend to the Prime Minister that he go to Washington to interview President Eisenhower, perhaps Senator Taft, certainly Mr. Dulles, and other congressional spokesmen in the hope that further unilateral action by the United States which may extend the conflict will not be embarked upon. I believe that such a trip by the Prime Minister would constitute a mission of peace. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs was not completely satisfied with the conversations he had-I hope he was-then the Prime Minister might consider such a visit because unless such action is taken now, some time later it may be too late.
I believe the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) emphasized very well this afternoon the need for economic assistance to underdeveloped countries. I believe that if we are
External Affairs
going to win friends for democracy, if we are going to win friends for the west, we should increase our economic and technical assistance to backward nations. I was really amazed at the figures the hon. member placed on the record, which if I remember correctly, indicated that since 1949 Canada's per capita contribution by way of economic aid and technical assistance has only been some $3.69 per capita, whereas the United States per capita contribution for the same purpose within the same period has been over $100. Canadians are a generous people. I believe they are willing to send surplus agricultural commodities and additional quantities of other goods from Canada. I believe they are willing that parliament should vote additional moneys for technical assistance in order to help those underdeveloped countries that are in a much less fortunate position than Canada. By so doing we would not only strengthen democratic institutions but we would be following good, sound, Christian principles.
From time to time I have read, as other members no doubt have, of the poverty, privation, distress, malnutrition, yes, starvation, rampant in Korea today. I believe we have a special obligation to assist the people of Korea. If they are short of food; if for example their children need larger quantities of milk, as I am sure they must, then certainly Canada is well able to provide the people of Korea with large quantities of foods that are now in surplus supply in this country. We have such a surplus of meat products and such a surplus of grain that farmers do not know how long the market can carry these commodities even at present prices, many of which are depressed. We have a surplus of 100 million pounds of meat that the government is holding. I think that provides us with a real opportunity to make available meat and grain to help prevent starvation and malnutrition in Korea. And the same applies to powdered milk.
As I have already said, we hope that no further steps will be taken that will lead to an extension of the war in Korea and that in the end might lead to an all-out war. I am particularly fearful that a unilateral blockade of China by the United States would be a step leading to all-out war. I would object to Canada's involvement in such a war, and the taking of Canadian youths from their normal peacetime occupations to be thrown into a conflagration on the continent of Asia.

I was not
absolutely certain, Mr. Speaker, that I wanted to take part in this debate, although I have not been totally unprepared, until I heard

External Affairs
speeches such as that delivered by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) earlier today and the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). If I had any doubts as to whether or not I should take part in this debate, those speeches resolved my doubts.
The doubts I had are those which any amateur must feel when he ventures, for not quite the first time but almost the first time, into a professional league. I have been watching the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) during the course of some of the speeches delivered in the last part of the debate, and I observed that the minister appears to feel somewhat uncomfortable. I could not help observing that. Probably the minister and I feel equally uncomfortable, but for completely opposite reasons.
I imagine the minister feels uncomfortable because he regrets that he was not more outspoken. He probably regrets that he minced so daintily around the field of foreign affairs, and refrained from enunciating more clearly just what is Canada's policy. I feel uncomfortable because I realize that if I were to make a definite statement, then I probably would be attacked as vigorously and from as many different quarters as the minister is now being attacked because he refrained from making a definite statement.
There are, Mr. Speaker, certain things which should be said. I go back in my mind to what the hon. member for Melfort said at the beginning of what was otherwise a fairly good speech. I think it is a shame if we are going to have to interrupt what appears to have been a modus vivendi established between ourselves and the members of the C.C.F. party by taking somewhat sharp issue with them in this field of foreign affairs. I feel that my friends of the C.C.F. party will have the same respect for my views if I feel compelled to express them as I have for theirs, and realize that it is an honest difference of opinion that moves us to say what we have to say in the course of this debate.
We did not call you yapping dogs as yet, did we?
I have not heard that expression used in the house.
Look up the speech of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson).
I was not in the house when the expression was used that appears to have somewhat disturbed my friends in the C.C.F. party. If it was used, I can only ask them to put it down to the heat of debate.
We seem to have disturbed you.

My hon. friend the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) may be disturbed, but I am equally disturbed by some of the things he has said in the course of this and preceding debates. I do not want to be bitter or to suggest that there has been disloyalty or anything of that kind. I want to discuss this thing on the basis of reality and common sense.
The hon. member for Melfort referred this afternoon to statements which have been made by members of this party in the course of this debate, and said that if Sir Robert Borden had been alive today he would have been disturbed to see the Conservative party apparently following-what he suggested, but what is not a fact-with slavish adulation the policy of President Eisenhower, the new president of the United States. Let me suggest to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party that what we are doing is not following this, that or the other lead from any foreign government, but we are trying to adopt a sane and sensible foreign policy which, if I may suggest to my hon. friends, will not be subject to the same vacillations as theirs.
We are not disturbed if we find that the governments of other countries, changing as they may do from time to time, adopt foreign policies which from time to time differ from that which we think should be the foreign policy of this country. If my hon. friend complains because for the time being there appears to be some difference between ourselves and some expressions used by the government of the United Kingdom in the approach to this problem of foreign policy with respect to the Asiatic sphere-well, I leave him to be concerned about that. I shall ask him, however, if in analysing the situation and accusing us of a shift in policy he would be kind enough to explain to us the complete shift in foreign policy which his own party has made with respect particularly to this Formosan situation.
I recall so vividly, Mr. Speaker, that in 1950, when President Truman announced his policy of controlling Formosa, there were no more bitter critics of that policy than my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party. Today, when President Eisenhower announced his decision to lift the ban, to take off the quarantine on Formosa, there are no more bitter critics of President Eisenhower's policy than my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party.
He only half lifted it.
The hon. member for Vancouver East objects because he says the quarantine has been only half removed. Imagine how much bitterer his criticism would have been if it had been totally removed.
Not at all.
What does my hon. friend want?
I do not want to get involved in a Chinese civil war.

You say you do not want to get involved in a Chinese civil war, and none of us does. What we are discussing here is a shift or what is alleged to be a shift in foreign policy. I am pointing out that when President Truman quarantined Formosa there were no more bitter critics of that policy than my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party. Now President Eisenhower has half lifted that quarantine-I use their own words-and they suggest President Eisenhower is deliberately involving us in the Chinese civil war.
