When President Truman applied the quarantine their great fear was that this might somehow or other involve us in a Chinese civil war, so I do not know what my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party want. They criticize us for what they allege to be the subservient following of the foreign policy of some other government when we try to pursue a consistent course and suggest that what is being done today by President Eisenhower is not such a great change after all, and that we should not allow ourselves, as they appear to be allowing themselves, to be influenced by a personal dislike of the present regime in the United States. They seem to be influenced by that personal dislike into criticizing a quite logical development in foreign policy.
You should not attribute motives.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Churchill takes the same position.

If I have attributed motives, then I apologize for doing so. Let me content myself with saying that we should not criticize the present policy of the United States government simply because it happens to be the policy of President Eisenhower and not that of President Truman.
A little earlier I said that the Secretary of State for External Affairs seems to be somewhat uncomfortable as a result of the criticism or speeches which have been made by members of the C.C.F. party who have spoken latterly in this debate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am perfectly comfortable.
Then the minister should develop more of a poker face.
Or the hon. member should get a pair of glasses.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am just exhausted.

I notice, Mr. Speaker, that the minister skated carefully around this subject of Formosa as dealt with by President
External Affairs
Eisenhower in his recent state of the union message to Congress, but he contrived to leave the impression that the Canadian government was not too happy about that policy. I am therefore afraid that we must associate him to some extent with the spokesmen for the C.C.F. party who have also criticized President Eisenhower's policy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister has to be right once in a while.

Yes; he has to be right once in a while. But I suggest that he has not been right yet. When this subject was discussed in the house in 1950 and the quarantine of Formosa was applied by President Truman, I recall that the minister expressed himself carefully but in terms which certainly implied that he was not happy about that policy. As reported at page 96 of Hansard of August 31, 1950 starting at page 95, he stated as follows:
We have, however, been disturbed, as I have no doubt others have been disturbed, by reports of preventive military measures taken by the nationalist government of China against communist concentrations along the mainland coast, as well as by statements reported to have been made by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek concerning United States-Chinese "military co-operation". We have also been disturbed by statements that seem in our minds to confuse the defence of Korea, which has been assumed by the United Nations, with the defence of Formosa, which has not;-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said that the other night.

To continue:
-statements that have even implied-somewhat mistakenly I think-that those who wish to draw at this time a distinction between the two operations are defeatists and appeasers. So far as this government is concerned, we are concerned solely with carrying out our United Nations obligations in Korea or elsewhere. These obligations do not, as I understand them at the present time, include anything that can be interpreted as the restoration of the nationalist Chinese government to the mainland of China, or an intervention in Formosa.
With that statement we perhaps could not find too much to disagree. But it is significant, Mr. Speaker, that that statement was made after President Truman had announced his policy of quarantining Formosa. Then President Eisenhower announced his policy of dequarantining Formosa, and we find the Secretary of State for External Affairs making almost the same statement as he made on the previous occasions. He finds fault with both policies. Neither of them suits him. But he does not tell us exactly what it is that he would have this government do, or rather what policy it is that he would have this country follow with respect to that matter.
When you read the debates, Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that at that time, in 1950, the minister's statement was taken as being quite

External Affairs
substantially critical of the policy adopted at the moment by the President of the United States; I refer to the policy of quarantining Formosa. In support of that contention I cite statements of members of the C.C.F. as well as statements of members of his own party. For instance, starting at page 173 of Hansard for the same session, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) delivered himself of a speech, in which he strongly criticized the Chiang Kai-shek government and suggested that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was quite right in criticizing the policy then followed by the President of the United States. At page 229 of Hansard the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) had much the same thing to say. At page 125 the leader of the C.C.F. party aligned himself fully with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had said. These were his words:
May I say before 1 take my seat how pleased I was yesterday when the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in discussing the Korean situation. made it abundantly clear that Canada was participating in the United Nations action in Korea, and that we were in no way involved in the Formosan situation. I said some time ago, and I now repeat, that the only thing to do-and it should have been done long ago-is to say to Chiang Kai-shek, "Get out of Formosa and stay out of Formosa", so as ultimately to give the Formosan people an opportunity to choose their own form of government-because they were once a free and independent people, and not so many decades ago at that.
He then went on to say:
I cannot go into that phase of the matter further except to say that the minister has the support at least of this group in the house in the attitude he has expressed from time to time in connection with Formosa, and the difficulties that have arisen in connection with it.
Some of the difficulties which the leader of the C.C.F. party was discussing were difficulties created by the announcement of President Truman with respect to Formosa; and it is difficulties with respect to the same situation which now cause the hon. gentleman to denounce the policy being followed by the United States in dequarantining Formosa. Yet the basis of their other criticism was that the quarantine of Formosa would involve us somehow in the Chinese civil war.
That was a position which, by inference if not by direct statement, was taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that at no time during the course of the debate in 1950 did he dissociate himself from the interpretation placed upon his position by the C.C.F. party. I therefore must assume that the hon. gentleman's position in 1950 was the same as the position expressed by the C.C.F. party at that time. Hence we find

that today, in 1953, when Formosa is de-quarantined, the Secretary of State for External Affairs expresses himself as being concerned

although not dotting the "i's" or crossing the "t's" as to the extent of his concern-over the possible implications of the President's policy.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What did he mean by "dequarantine"?

I should think that was reasonably obvious, Mr. Speaker. When you apply a quarantine, you post a notice and say that no one will be allowed to come into this house. When you dequarantine, you take down the notice and say that this house is no longer subject to quarantine.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The notice has not been taken down.

The minister says the notice has not been taken down. I do not know what interpretation he places upon the President's message to the Congress of the United States. Perhaps he will be good enough to explain to us when he closes the debate-as I presume he will-just what interpretation he places on it.
At any rate, whatever interpretation he places on it, the fact is that the message has given him cause for some concern; and I should be greatly interested to know whether or not the cause for concern which it gives him is the same cause for concern, and the same inconsistent cause for concern, as it gives to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party, namely that somehow or other, by some strange transmutation of all the processes of international relations, the very opposite of the act which was alleged in 1950 would involve us in the Chinese civil war, in 1953 is going to have the same result.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has involved himself in other difficulties in connection with this matter. They are difficulties perhaps of a minor nature; nevertheless they are significant when highlighted against the background of the whole government policy.
These difficulties that are referred to at the moment are in connection with the interpretation we place upon the seriousness of this whole war in Korea. I do not want to be overly captious, although the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) accused me of that fault at an earlier stage of this debate, particularly in respect to my criticisms of the government. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to adopt a tone

which is offensive, because we have been told that if our tone is not exactly suited to the sensitive ears of the government, then they may not care to sit here and listen to us. Therefore if my tone is offensive I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others of his colleagues in the cabinet will let me know, and I shall attempt to modulate the tone to their delicate sensibilities.
What I have in mind is that the other night the Secretary of State for External Affairs objected to a criticism which I advanced against the use of the words "police action" to describe the present war in Korea. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, placing a reliance upon a magazine which, as he himself pointed out, is better known for its humorous qualities than for its biblical authority in the field of international affairs, proceeded to quote from the New Yorker. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs had quoted from the New York Times, which we have always been given to understand is the authorized version of the bible in so far as the formulation of government policy on foreign affairs is concerned, I would have been more impressed, but he chose to quote from the New Yorker in justification of his description of the action in Korea as a police action.
I was interested this afternoon when the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Rooney) addressed a question to the government as to whether or not we are at war. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), giving a very cautious answer, said in the course of his reply that the question might better have been directed either to the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs. When he said that I could'not help but think that he should have said the question should have been directed both to the Prime Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because undoubtedly he would have obtained a different answer from each of the hon. gentlemen.
Although the fact is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs saw fit to disagree with me and criticize me for having taken exception to the description of the war in Korea as a police action, the Prime Minister leaves no doubt that in his opinion that in which we are engaged in Korea is a war. The Secretary of State for External Affairs prefers to describe it in 1953 as a police action; but I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that when he spoke in this house not very long ago the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 1524 of Hansard:
We do agree that if war were not being waged in Korea, a war which might have serious consequences for the free world at large, young Cana-
External Affairs
dians would not be voluntarily offering up their services and risking their lives for something of the character of an ordinary police action.
I wonder which the Secretary of State for External Affairs is going to take as his authority, the Prime Minister or the New Yorker magazine. On humorous subjects I would be willing to agree with him that the New Yorker might speak with a voice of greater authority, but I should think that in this house a colleague in the cabinet would prefer to accept the authoritative pronouncement of the Prime Minister. But of course if the Secretary of State for External Affairs is implying that the statements of the Prime Minister are humorous in their nature, even dealing with a serious subject of this sort, well, who am I to quarrel with him? I do hope the hon. gentleman will reconcile not only the very marked difference of interpretation between himself and the Prime Minister in these two speeches, but will also reconcile for us the difference in his attitude in 1953 from what he said when he dealt with this subject in 1950.
I might point out to the hon. gentleman and to the hon. gentleman who is sitting with him at the moment, and who I presume is equally interested in this debate, that in 1950 when he dealt with this subject the Secretary of State for External Affairs on no fewer than four occasions referred to what was going on in Korea as a war, and on two occasions as a military challenge and on another occasion as the conflict in Korea. I do not recall that at any time on that occasion he described it as a police action. Here is what he said as reported on page 91 of Hansard of August 31, 1950. After having described the developments which led up to the outbreak of war in Korea he said:
This is the perspective in which we must view the war in Korea today, though I do not for a moment suggest that these considerations should lessen our anxiety over those events or block our response to them. In Korea, together with the other countries of the free world, we are now faced with a plain and unmistakable military challenge; and we, in common with all the free world, must answer that challenge.
Then further down on the same page he said:
It was possible in Korea, as it has been possible elsewhere, for the war to be fought by satellites, by Asian troops alone. Therefore, when the United Nations intervened, the war could be misrepresented, as it has been misrepresented, as one of Asian popular forces against those of western imperialist capitalism.
On page 94 the Secretary of State for External Affairs had this to say in referring

External Affairs
to the Canadian brigade which was being sent to Korea to take part in a war, not a police action:
This special force is unique in one way among the offers of military forces which have been made to the United Nations as the result of the war in Korea-
Well now, Mr. Speaker, viewed in the light of the last situation with which we are confronted it is perhaps a fairly small matter as to whether we describe it as a war or a police action; except that I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the consequences of this situation which has resulted in a war in Korea are too grave for us to take casually and in the mincing attitude the Secretary of State for External Affairs has adopted toward them.
After all, the President of the United States has said certain things with regard to United States policy with respect to the communist threat confronting the world today. I think it is truthful to say he indicated that he intends, in so far as his government is concerned, to adopt a certain policy with respect to that question, a policy which reverses the position in which his government has found itself in the past, as he says, of always having to come from behind and deal with a situation provoked by the communists, instead of trying to take the initiative, always within the limit of peaceful means, and within the limits of peaceful means trying instead to keep the communists guessing.
It seems to me, when our troops are engaged in war in Korea, I say as the Prime Minister said a few days ago:
We do agree that if war were not being waged in Korea, a war which might have serious consequences for the free world at large, young Canadians would not be voluntarily offering up their services and risking their lives for something of the character of an ordinary police action.
I say when we are faced with that situation it is high time for us to stop fiddling around and saying, on the one hand, that what President Truman did in 1950 might have involved us in civil war in China, and then saying that fatal action has been taken by the President of the United States in 1953 that might well involve us in civil war in China.
It is time we stopped fiddling about and wearying-well, I will not say wearying of the foreign policies of other countries, because obviously we have to be concerned with their foreign policies-but it is time we stopped trying to criticize the foreign policies of other countries in order to make political advantage for ourselves here at home. It is time we adopted a policy consistent with our traditional position as a member of the commonwealth.
Goodness knows, from time to time we may find ourselves having differences of opinion with other nations in the commonwealth, but let us not be dismayed when that happens. That simply means that we just have to sit down around a table, as this government has done all too seldom, and iron out those differences. We just have to try to find a common denominator in commonwealth foreign policy, and reconcile that foreign policy with the foreign policy of the United States, always recognizing honest differences but not carping at them simply because they happen to have changed their president.
Let us go forward so that, within the framework of the United Nations and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization we may have a foreign policy which will prevent our always being on the defence in the cold war. I say again, within the limits of peaceful means at our disposal let us make certain that, for a change, the communists are kept guessing in this cold war instead of, in the company of our allies and our friends, always having to come from behind, with no preconceived idea of what we must do to prevent a further extension of communist success in this sphere.
I have said it is not easy for the inexpert to venture in where the experts themselves are somewhat at a loss. But I said at the outset that I hope my hon. friends, particularly those in the C.C.F., would not take it amiss if I appear to differ somewhat sharply from their views.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We do not object to that; but we do wish you would state your own views.

I have stated them. I have just said that I believe Canada, in concert with other nations of the commonwealth and, in so far as it is possible, with the United States of America, should adopt a foreign policy which would carry not the hot war but the cold war to the communists, and keep them guessing for a change. Let us do that, instead of always having the reverse situation, in which the communists have been carrying the cold war to us and keeping us guessing.
If that statement is not sufficiently definite for my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I hope he will elaborate upon his views so I may have the benefit of knowing just where he stands, and of understanding that the views expressed in this debate by his party are not formulated solely and simply because there has been a change in the presidency of that great nation to the south of us, the United States of America.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the remarks I shall make

in this foreign affairs debate will be unique in that they will be the briefest. My only reason for rising is to make it perfectly clear that there are two things in respect of which the people in the Fraser valley stand united. First, we hate war; second, we believe the United Nations is the best hope we have to prevent war.
I am sorry my hon. friends of the Social Credit party apparently do not agree with me in either case. We have had a small influx of their numbers into our province, and I want to impress upon them that, possibly because from personal experience we have a deep appreciation of war and because we hate war, we want to prevent it; and we think the best way of preventing it is through the United Nations.
We in the Fraser valley have not forgotten Great Britain and her allies who are facing a most difficult time. We have not forgotten men like the late President Roosevelt who, under lend-lease, saw to it that we got the destroyers when we needed them most. We have not forgotten that. And as Canadians in the Fraser valley we always regarded President Roosevelt as the greatest friend Canada ever had.
Nor have we forgotten President Truman, and the manner in which he co-operated with us. Let us not forget that long before his country was at war, President Roosevelt was standing behind us and behind Great Britain. The policy of the Social Credit party is that set out at page 1881 of Hansard, where their leader said:
-the past two presidents-
And we do not forget that this would include Mr. Winston Churchill, too.
-of the United States have been the great betrayers of humanity.
We cannot understand a party, through its leader, enunciating a policy like that, which attacks men like Roosevelt and Truman after all they have done, and describes them as the great betrayers of humanity.
As I have said, we in the Fraser valley, and I believe the people throughout British Columbia, believe that our great hope to prevent future wars lies in the United Nations. But the second lieutenant of the Social Credit party-or perhaps he is the corporal-said, at page 1938 of Hansard:
The fact of the matter is that this United Nations is largely a socialist-communist organization.
Well, I think that is an insult to the people of Canada and the people of the whole free world. It is an insult when any man tells me that our Secretary of State for External
External Affairs
Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is a socialist or a communist, or that the representatives from Great Britain are socialists or communists. There have been suggested changes in the rules of the house. I would hope they might be modified so that I would be permitted to answer in language that should be used.
I said I would be brief, and I shall be. In the Fraser valley we do not want war, and we believe that the best way to prevent it is by supporting, not attacking, the United Nations.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-
When the minister speaks he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This has been a most interesting debate. A good many points have arisen during it, with some of which at least I am sure the house will expect me to deal. Before doing so, however, I should like sincerely to thank hon. members who were good enough to congratulate me during the course of the debate upon my election to the presidency of the United Nations general assembly. I shall be going back there in a day or two; and during the course of the resumed session I know that I shall listen once again to a great many very long speeches, with all of which I shall certainly not agree. While I am in the chair I shall have the opportunity to speculate, speculation which would certainly be out of place in this house, as to which is the more important, freedom of speech or freedom from speeches.
I should like to follow the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) in what I must confess I considered to be his somewhat tortuous reasoning as to the difference between police action and war, and also in his attempt, which so far as I was concerned was not successful-possibly because I was not very bright-to decide when a quarantine is put on and when it is taken off. I suggest to him that if he studies the terms of President Truman's quarantine in 1950 and the terms of President Eisenhower's statement the other day he will realize that only half the quarantine has been lifted. When a quarantine is lifted so that people can leave the quarantined house but nobody can enter, that is not dequarantining as I understand it.
Would the minister say-
Sit down.
You made your speech.

Would the minister say whether he agrees with the President's policy, or does he think that President Eisenhower should have gone further?

External Affairs

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will deal with that in a minute if the hon. gentleman will be just half as patient with me as I tried to be with him. One subj ect came up in the debate which I think was unfortunate, and this was dealt with by other speakers. I refer to the statement made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and to certain observations made this afternoon by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). So far as the reputation of and the verdict on President Roosevelt and President Truman are concerned, I think we can leave that to history. When all the facts are known and the judgment is written I feel quite certain that the verdict will not be that which has been suggested in this house-that he should be considered as being a betrayer of humanity. President Roosevelt was one of the great defenders of humanity. I also like to think that when history is written it will find a more adequate source of material than the memoirs of Mr. Elliott Roosevelt.
I am sure that Mr. Winston Churchill will be most interested in the observations of the hon. member for Macleod this afternoon that at the conferences which were attended by him and President Roosevelt, the latter spent most of his time making Mr. Churchill squirm. Mr. Churchill does not squirm easily.
In the article to which so much attention has been directed in this debate and which was written by the hon. member for Macleod -I think he has authenticated the article- he indicated that he was turning the searchlight on truth on certain things. Therefore he must naturally expect to be judged pretty critically when he himself states that he is turning that searchlight on the United Nations. He also said during the course of his statement that if there were demonstrated inaccuracies in that article he would withdraw them, but not until they were demonstrated to be inaccurate. That is a fair observation on his part.
I shall just point out to him without any further explanation one inaccuracy which has been pointed out in the last few minutes. In that article he described the United Nations as being largely a socialist-communist organization. I am taking just a few of his statements at random. He also said that Mr. Alger Hiss was the executive secretary of the Bretton Woods conference. Third, he said in that article that Mr. Hiss's advisers-Mr. Hiss was a middle-ranking civil servant at that time-were Henry Morgenthau, Jr., the secretary of the treasury; Mr. James P. Warburg, Mr. Eugene Meyer, and a man with a Scotch name, Mr. John J. McCloy, who he said sat under the teaching of the marxist Felix Frankfurter of Harvard Law School,

Felix Frankfurter being a very distinguished justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. I would hope that at an appropriate opportunity the hon. member for Macleod will admit that some of those statements are demonstrably inaccurate.
My own contribution to this debate up to the present has been governed, as I meant it to be governed, by the fact that I speak with the responsibility of a member of the government charged with external affairs. When I am criticized, as I was criticized this evening by the hon. member for Kamloops, for my casual and mincing attitude toward this matter, I realize that I do not speak with his freedom from official responsibility. It has also been suggested by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon)-I am sorry he is not in the house tonight-that my earlier statement might be described as tiptoeing among the tulips.
There were at least two members of my hon. friend's group-the leaders of what I have called the dynamic wing of that group, the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green)-who were certainly doing no tiptoeing in their statements. I hope I am not doing them an injustice when I suggest that they seemed to have adopted as a principle for the conduct of diplomacy and international affairs what I might call tulip trampling or gatecrashing. If they had had the same limitation of responsibility that I had when I spoke here they might possibly agree that in the delicate situation, such as that in which we find ourselves today in the Far East and Korea and in connection with international relations generally, the behaviour of the Secretary of State for External Affairs should be to tiptoe carefully and not trample the tulips.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in a most interesting contribution to the debate criticized my statement as being too optimistic, or very optimistic, as he described it. I think in that earlier contribution my optimism was indeed most limited, as it was meant to be. The hon. member for Lake Centre contrasted what he called my great optimism with the view of a much greater authority on foreign affairs than I, or any of us possibly-Mr. Winston Churchill. But it was only a few weeks ago that Mr. Winston Churchill when landing in New York stated to the press that in his view the danger of war had receded. If Mr. Churchill saw fit to take a more sombre view of international developments the other day in the House of Commons in London, this

merely shows the difficulty of making up one's mind during the ebb and flow of international events.
As a matter of fact we have no cause at this time for either optimism or despair. This afternoon the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) made what I thought was a very interesting and thoughtful contribution to this debate. In referring to the situation in western Europe he said that because of the growing strength of NATO the situation in western Europe had been stabilized and the Soviet union was at bay. I certainly would not go as far as that, and possibly he did not mean to go as far as his words might indicate.
I suggest that we should avoid both excessive optimism and excessive pessimism. We should not get too cheerful when things seem to go well or too panicky when they seem to go badly.
In the course of our discussion the question of our policy toward the United Nations was brought up by more than one speaker, and the very interesting proposal was made by more than one member of the official opposition that it would be a good thing if the standing committee on external affairs set up a group or a subcommittee to discuss, no doubt with the department and its officials, the revision of the United Nations chartef which in any event has to be discussed at the United Nations general assembly before the tenth session. I think that is a good idea, and I hope that possibly the standing committee on external affairs will follow it up when it meets.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) thought that in order to relieve the general assembly of the growing pressure of business, which is resulting now in two sessions every year, there should be set up at the United Nations an agenda committee which would screen the subjects for discussion at each general assembly and thereby reduce the number of subjects and I hope the time devoted to them. If he were here I would have pointed out to him that this has been tried more than once at the United Nations general assembly. Proposals have been made for the establishment of such a committee, but they have never met with enough approval to be given a trial. As a matter of fact there are obvious difficulties in a proposal of that kind because in the screening process some subjects might be left out which might be of very great importance to some countries, though not so much to others, and it would be extremely difficult to take away from any national delegation the right to put any subject on the agenda.
External Affairs
Then in our discussion more than one speaker referred to the problems about the United Nations secretariat. In fact the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) devoted most of his speech to that subject. There is an impression being created in some quarters that the United Nations is honeycombed with subversive agents and that the security of the host country is being prejudiced by the secretariat. My own view is that that impression has no basis in reality at all, and I think it is deplorable that it should be spreading so widely over the continent.
The hon. member for Lake Centre also touched on this subject. He underlined the difficulties in dealing with security not only in the United Nations but also at home when he said-and the same comment was made by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) 

that while we must maintain our freedoms unimpaired, which I think was the expression he used, we must at the same time not allow diplomatic immunity to be used to attack the security of the state. The difficulty of course is to reconcile these two things. We cannot allow freedom to be used to destroy security, but we would surely be making a great mistake if we took unnecessary measures in the name of security which would destroy our freedom. What we have to do in these matters, I suppose, both internationally at the United Nations and domestically at home, is to make a reasonable and wise reconciliation between these two matters.
So far as attacks on the United Nations secretariat are concerned, we must not forget that they are often made by people who are really attacking the United Nations itself. When attacks are made on United States citizens in the United Nations, you will often find behind them attacks on the fact that the United States is in the United Nations at all. It is an important problem. It is on the agenda of the resumed session, when it will be discussed; and I think it would probably not be quite appropriate for me to say anything more about it at this time.
It is in this spirit, however, of attempting to reconcile freedom and security that in the Department of External Affairs we attempt to deal with passport difficulties, a question which was also raised by the hon. member for Peel. In our passport policies-and we have discussed these at great length before the standing committee on external affairs, as I have no doubt we will discuss them again this year-I confess we have followed the British rather than the United States practice. We interfere only on very rare occasions with the right of a Canadian citizen

External Affairs
to possess a passport, which is after all merely a certificate of his Canadian citizenship. We have the power, of course, to refuse a passport or to withdraw a passport, and when the danger to the state is immediate and clear we should of course take that action; and it has been taken within recent years. But I suggest that we should interfere just as little as possible with the right of a Canadian to have this certificate of identity.
The hon. member for Peel brought up four or five other questions which he hoped I could deal with in my reply. I think possibly they should be referred to the standing committee, where all information concerning them can be given. He mentioned, for instance, the case of a Canadian citizen of Polish extraction-indeed a Polish national as well because he had dual nationality-who had received what seemed to the Auditor General exorbitant sums for relief in Warsaw in circumstances which appeared to be a little ambiguous. I think that case can be satisfactorily explained to the committee in all its details. I would only say here that this Polish-Canadian citizen served during the war in the Canadian navy, where he had a good record. He went back to Poland after the war in the hope that he could bring his wife and family to Canada. There he was arrested by the Polish authorities. After he was released from jail he was destitute. The Canadian diplomatic mission in Warsaw felt it was its duty to help this man until his case was cleared up. Relief was extended. It might seem to be a large amount, but the amount in dollars was converted at the official diplomatic rate to zlotys which, in terms of real value, would cut it in half. As I say, we can go into this particular question in the standing committee in enough detail, I think, to satisfy hon. members of the committee.
The hon. member for Peel also hoped that I could say something about the C.B.C. international service. He suggested that we call the director of that service before the committee. I think that is a good suggestion. I am quite sure it can be acted on and that we can go into the whole question, as indeed we have done before, of the relationship between the Department of External Affairs and the C.B.C. international service. The hon. member did go a little further than I thought was practical when he expressed the hope that we might listen to recordings of the broadcasts we are making to these countries. He may be more cultivated linguistically than I am, but I think recordings in Ukrainian, Polish, Czechoslovakian and other languages would not be very meaningful, at least so far as I am concerned.
The hon. member for Lake Centre made a very interesting suggestion in connection with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. He thought we should take the lead in the extension of the pact from 20 to 50 years. It is now a 20-year pact which can be renewed after the 20-year period indefinitely from year to year. The European defence community treaty is a 50-year pact. It was felt that if we could make the two agreements synchronize that would help to remove some of the uneasiness, particularly in France, over this matter.
As a matter of fact that question is already under discussion. There is a difficulty at this time in extending the North Atlantic treaty to 50 years because it would mean a formal amendment of the pact, which would have to go back to the 14 legislatures. There may be a better way than that of accomplishing the same purpose, but the question is under consideration at the present time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, though all these matters arose during the course of the debate, and many others, the question of most interest to hon. members quite naturally was that of Korea, Formosa and the Far East generally -the question of our Far Eastern policy at the present time.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), in discussing my observations on this question, criticized them as being without substance. He described part of my remarks on President Eisenhower's statement about Formosa as a masterpiece of circumlocution. Well, I listened to his statement very carefully-I am sorry he is not in his seat tonight-and I read his statement in Hansard very carefully. In a friendly vein I should like to return the compliment and suggest that his own statement was a masterpiece of concealment.
The hon. member said that the opposition, in discussing foreign affairs, should put forward alternative suggestions. I certainly agree with that. Then he added-without which a discussion on foreign affairs would be as shadowy as it would be meaningless. I have gone through his speech, as I have stated, and I have gone through several speeches by hon. members on the other side to see if I could get some of these alternative suggestions. I have not been very successful in finding them. It is not easy, therefore, for me to take the constructive advice that I should like to secure from the statements made by members of the opposition on this occasion, except in one or two speeches with which I shall deal later.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) made the same criticism and he, but more

particularly the hon. member for Lake Centre, in a very eloquent and rhetorical bit, said that this house and this country had the right to know where we stood on Far Eastern matters. He went on to prove his point by stating that the people of the United States knew where their government stood, as did the people of the United Kingdom through Mr. Eden's statement, and that we in Canada should also know.
I have taken the trouble to read Mr. Eden's statements, the one he made on February 3 and the one he made in the House of Commons on February 9. Dealing with the Formosa decision on February 3, he said that Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom were informed in advance of the decision of the United States government and at once made known their concern at this decision which they feared would have unfortunate political repercussions without compensating military advantages. In his statement a few days later in the House of Commons, Mr. Eden spoke at some length on this Formosa decision. He explained some of the United States preoccupations, difficulties and worries. He deprecated the exaggeration of the implications of this action. He reiterated the British policy on the blockade, and he mentioned the cease-fire proposals; but comparing his statement with the statement of government policy made in this house I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we were as definite and I think went just about as far as Mr. Eden did.
I propose to put on the record again one or two of the things I have said, representing the government, in my last two statements on this subject.
So far as the United States is concerned, I have just come back from Washington. Of course I read the United States papers, the New York Times and even the New Yorker. I am afraid there are a good many people in the United States who do not feel that they know exactly where their government stands on these Far Eastern matters and who might, with charity, consider that the Canadian people are just about as well informed in respect of the policy of their government on this particular question.
On February 5, when I spoke in the house on the Formosan statement I said, as recorded at page 1639 of Hansard-and I refer this to the hon. member for Kamloops because it repeats almost verbatim what I said almost two years ago on the subject-
-while we remain resolved to carry out our United Nations obligations in Korea, we do not think that the defence of Formosa, which has not been assumed by the United Nations, should be confused with the defence of Korea, which has.
I think that is clear.
External Affairs
You said the same thing on both occasions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On the same occasion and on the same page I said:
We are not of course committed by, though naturally we are concerned with, the action taken in Washington in connection with this matter.
We are not committed by it, though naturally we are concerned with it. The words Mr. Eden used in London were "at once made known our concern." I recall that when I used the word "concern" in a diplomatic note not many months ago in connection with a Far Eastern question, that was considered by hon. gentlemen opposite to be a very vigorous protest indeed. It was not a very vigorous protest then, and it is not a protest at all on this occasion, but it is a good word to use in a situation such as this. We are concerned with this matter, and we have made our concern known to the United States.
It has been suggested by hon. members opposite that in my Wednesday statement I was much less definite and more tiptoeing than in my previous one. On that occasion, to make our position as clear as I think it should be at this time, I said, as recorded on page 1852 of Hansard for February 11, 1953:
The guiding principle of Canadian policy in Korea is to continue to do everything possible to limit the present hostilities to the Korean peninsula, and to take advantage of any opportunity for an early settlement of these hostilities by peaceful negotiation.
Farther down on the same page I said:
We consider also that the purpose of the United Nations in Korea remains the defeat of aggression there, and does not include intervention in the civil war in China.
On the next page, I said:
We do not believe, accordingly, that the western powers should press for military or economic measures, at the United Nations or elsewhere, which would certainly not be supported and indeed might be actively opposed by important non-communist Asian states, and which without such support would be less effective in ending the Korean war than in extending it.
Then I added:
This principle has guided our policy in this matter in the past, and it will continue to guide us in considering any such proposals which may be made in the future.
It seemed to me, Mr. Speaker, that those were fairly definite statements. We expressed our concern with these Formosan declarations; we expressed our anxiety lest anything should be done which would extend the war from Korea to the mainland; and we underlined the contrast between action taken through the United Nations and action taken in other ways. So far as consultation is concerned, immediately this declaration was

External Affairs
decided upon by the United States government as a unilateral action-though I confess we had some advance information that some such action was in contemplation-we were informed by that government at once, as other governments were. We took steps at once through our ambassador in Washington to make immediate inquiries as to what it involved, what the implications were, if any, and to discuss the matter with the state department. Immediately after those discussions in Washington the ambassador came to Ottawa and we got a firsthand report from him. I think the consultation on this occasion was not anything that we could complain about, though if it had been possible to announce the step to us a little earlier we would have had more time to intervene, if we had felt that intervention was desirable; something that we did not feel on this occasion.
I only say that we-I mean the government-regret, as I think do most members of the house, that the United States government found it necessary to take this action. We are not condemning them for it, but we regret that they felt it necessary to take this action, the military advantages of which might be neutralized by the political disadvantages.
At the same time I think it is only right to state that the situation in 1953 with respect to the neutralization of Formosa, and the situation generally in that area is very different from that in 1950 when the original action was taken. At that time the Chinese communists had not directly intervened in the Korean struggle. Since then many an effort has been made through the United Nations to settle this conflict, and all of them have been rejected by the communists in China or in North Korea.
I had the privilege of spending the week end in Washington, and yesterday I had an interesting, friendly and frank discussion with the Secretary of State, Mr. Dulles, at our embassy there. I told him in an informal but frank way-and we are on those terms in Washington with the new Secretary of State, as we were with the old secretary of state- our views and our preoccupations. I told him quite clearly-something which his officials of course already knew-how we felt about Far Eastern affairs generally, and I think we have also made that clear in the house. I also learned from him about the background of this action, and of the preoccupations and worries which prompted the United States to take it. I think we should do our best to understand the United States position on this matter and to appreciate their anxiety over the stalemate which has

developed. I also think they should appreciate, as I think they do, our anxiety over the possibility of this war extending and our desire to prevent that eventuality.
The exchange of views that we had yesterday, I think, without exaggerating their importance, may have been considered helpful in that respect. It was made quite clear to me yesterday by the Secretary of State that some of the far-reaching fears that had been read into this action and other actions are not justified; that they are naturally exceedingly anxious to take advantage of any situation which will give them and the United Nations-because they are acting as a member of the United Nations in this general Korean situation-the initiative, and also to do anything they can to keep the enemies of the United Nations off balance. I feel reasonably assured that there is no intention on the part of the administration in Washington to do anything that is rash, provocative or adventurous, and that on their part they have no desire to extend the war to the continent of Asia.
I also feel that, like their predecessors in Washington, they appreciate the necessity and the desirability of consultation before decisions are taken in Washington which affect the other members of the United Nations who, whether or not they are committed formally by those decisions, cannot escape the consequences of them. Mr. Dulles, the Secretary of State, made a broadcast the other night, to which I am sure a good many hon. members listened, in which he said:
It is important for us all to remember that we-
And he was talking about the American people.
-do carry a tremendous responsibility. Any false step could mean disaster not only for us but for our friends. Possibly our friends would suffer even more than we ourselves. Therefore, we must be sober and restrained in our national conduct.
Then in concluding his broadcast he went on to say this:
That does not mean being timid, and afraid to take the initiative, to speak frankly or to make hard decisions. Indecision, weakness and vacillation are the qualities which most often lead to war. It does mean that in order to win and hold the confidence of those whom we need as friends and allies, we must at all times play the part of a nation which is fully aware of the grave responsibility which it carries.
I am sure that when the Secretary of State uttered those words he was sincere in his own determination to do his best to carry them out. I am reinforced in that feeling by my visit to Washington.
The other day, in his speech in this debate, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said we should let the United

External Affairs
States know that they cannot count on support from us in every political adventure into which their political exigencies at home may lead them. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I think they know that. But I also think it would be wrong at this time to assume, on the basis of the decision taken with respect to Formosa, that they are going to engage in such adventures. I do not think it would be wise, in our relations with this new administration, to start on a note of suspicion or controversy, if we can avoid it, any more than I think it would be wise to start by giving them the feeling that they can count on us on all occasions, no matter what they may be impelled to do. In this connection 1 think we would be well advised to distinguish-if we can, and it is not always as easy as it should be-between official statements on behalf of the administration and newspaper reports of statements by military leaders who seem to do a good deal of talking in one way or another-
In both countries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-and by civilians who have not the responsibility for their statements that members of the administration have and who recently have been making some statements which I confess are rather alarming. Mr. Dulles himself, in the broadcast to which I referred, had this to say on that point:
The talks which we had with the political leaders of the countries we visited-
He was talking about his visit to Europe.
-went far, I think, to dispel these fears in so far as official quarters are concerned.
He was talking about some fears that had been aroused by what had been going on. He went on to say:
However, the public and the opposition parties seize upon incidents and upon statements made here-
That is in the United States.
-which seem to them to be reckless. Unscrupulous persons use such incidents and statements as reasons why the European nations should not trust us.
I therefore hope that we shall be careful to differentiate between unofficial statements which often get on the front page and more important official statements which are not always on the front page.
On motion of Mr. Pearson the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall conclude this debate. Then we shall revert to notices of motion and take up the motion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to set up a special committee to examine into the operations of the government in the field of atomic energy; then the resolution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) with respect to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944; Bill No. 48, respecting food, drugs, cosmetics and therapeutic devices; Bill No. 44, to protect the coastal fisheries; Bill No. 46, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act; then the resolution respecting confirmation of the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, signed by Canada, the United States and Japan.
It being two minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
